EntertainmentTab.title: Girl group Katseye are missing two members, but their tour still dazzles
EntertainmentTab.text:
They may have been two members down, but the pop group Katseye received a hero's welcome as they played their first full concert in the UK.

The audience erupted with screams even before the show began, as the band broadcast their music videos on the O2 Arena's big screens, and the noise barely dipped for the next three hours.

It was proof that Katseye have become pop's biggest property (they're currently the most-streamed act on YouTube UK) even while singers Manon Bannerman and Sophia Laforteza are on health-related hiatus.

The stage felt emptier without them, but their bandmates worked hard to fill the gaps, hyping up the crowd with a succession of bass-heavy pop anthems and jaw-dropping dance breaks.

"Are you happy to see us?" asked the band's youngest member, Yoonchae Jeong, as if the answer hadn't been obvious from the moment they appeared in a storm of laser lights and launched into the Brazilian funk workout of Hootie Frutti.

"I think you guys are our loudest crowd ever, literally," marvelled Megan Skiendiel.

"This crowd is unbelievable," added Lara Raj.

The concert was only the second date of the band's Wildworld tour - but fans already knew every twist and turn from social media.

There was even a cheer of relief when Daniela Avanzini survived a complicated lift in the dance routine for Gabriella. On the opening night, her dance partner dropped her., external

Such adulation - and scrutiny - has come quickly for Katseye.

Based in Los Angeles, the multinational girl group were only formed in 2023 as part of the online reality competition show The Debut: Dream Academy.

The contest was created by Hybe, the South Korean entertainment company behind acts like BTS and Le Sserafim, and the US record label Geffen, home to Olivia Rodrigo and the Rolling Stones. Of the 120,000 who initially applied for the show, only six made it through.

Trained under the rigorous K-Pop system, they had a breakout year in 2025, first with the hyperactive electro-skronk of their single Gnarly, then with its follow-up, a slinky ballad called Gabriela that highlighted Daniela's Cuban-Venezuelan roots.

In London, their audience skewed young: The queue for pick and mix was longer than the one for the bar.

When Megan asked, "Whose first concert is this?" the air curdled with screams.

Throughout the show, fans shook lightsticks, parroted Katseye's dance moves and, in some cases, spontaneously burst into tears.

Many concert-goers also wore bindis, inspired by Lara, who has proudly incorporated her Asian heritage into her aesthetic.

One individual also came dressed as a courgette, a reference to Internet Girl's so-weird-it-almost-works refrain, "Eat zucchini".

The energy was infectious. And, if you looked closely, the parents were enjoying the show as much as their kids.

Even Spice Girl Melanie C is a fan, hosting a Q&A with the band during their first UK trip last October.

"They're incredible girls," she told the BBC earlier this summer. "They've got great music, they've got a great work ethic, and they're really beautiful, you know?

"Obviously, they've had a little drama, as happens with all bands, but they work so goddamn hard."

The drama began in February, when Manon announced she was taking a hiatus from the band to "focus on her health and wellbeing".

It came after the Swiss-Ghanaian singer told BBC News the band had been subject to racism and death threats; but fans also highlighted Katseye's gruelling schedule, suggesting they were being overworked.

In April, she posted a message to fans saying she was having "positive conversations" with Katseye's management, but not before she removed references to the band from her Instagram biography.

Then, just months after Manon stepped back, Sophia announced she was also going on hiatus to protect her "mental health and wellness".

"You can't pour from an empty cup," she posted on social media. "It's important to care for yourself."

Although it was hoped Sophia would return for the European leg of the Wildworld tour, that's proved impossible.

Her mother assured fans the absence is only temporary.

"Don't worry, this is for her own good," she told ABS-CBN News, external. "This is what I love about her management. They realise when the girls are tired.

"It's a good thing that she is resting so that she's stronger when she comes back."

It is not unusual for members of K-Pop bands to take a break when the mental or physical demands of the job become overwhelming.

Lia from the girl group Itzy took more than a year off work to seek treatment for "extreme levels of anxiety" in 2023-24; while Moka, a singer from Katseye's labelmates Illit, is currently on extended hiatus, also for anxiety.

In keeping with K-Pop tradition, Katseye honoured Sophia's place in the band during Tuesday's show, retaining her pre-recorded vocals on songs like Mean Girls and Pinky Up.

Manon's lyrics, however, were sung by other members of the band - presumably because her hiatus pre-dated production and rehearsals

Other highlights included Daniela's death-defying dance break, complete with aerial splits, that led into Gabriella; and Megan's technotronic shakedown at the end of Pinky Up.

For Yoonchae, the show's high point was Time Lapse, where she got to sing in her native Korean, while mingling with the crowd. ("Keep your hands to yourselves and don't throw any gifts on the stage for our safety," warned Lara, spoiling the atmosphere just a little).

The show ended on a powerful note, with Iconic By Mistake - the band's defiant response to an online hate campaign - and an extended romp through Gnarly, complete with a leather-studded rock remix.

All told, it was a stunningly confident and self-assured show from a band who could easily been diminished by personnel problems.

"This is not a goodbye," promised Yooncahe as Katseye waved goodbye. "We'll come back."

Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage would be a perfect fit.

EntertainmentTab.title: 'Not only did I survive, I thrived' - Meera Syal after assaults
EntertainmentTab.text:
Dame Meera Syal has said she "almost gave up" her career after being sexually harassed and assaulted by two "predators" within the media industry.

"I was out of work, I was homeless, sleeping on people's floors, and then these two things happened in quite quick succession," the Wolverhampton-born star said in a candid interview with BBC Asian Network's Amber Haque.

In her new memoir, Vigilauntie, which was published on Thursday, the actress shared that both incidents happened in her 20s, as she was struggling to secure a role.

Now aged 65, she has opened up about the harrowing experiences and reflected on how she overcame them to become one of the most well-known faces on British TV.

"It could have been a point where I gave up," she explained.

"It put some fire in my belly because the reason I wanted to tell these stories is that I did survive, and not only did I survive, I thrived.

"The anger of the injustice of the situation made me seek out a bunch of women that changed the course of my life."

Syal described the first incident as "my first casting couch approach".

She wrote that the man, a theatre director, insinuated he would give her a role in a pantomime if she engaged in sexual acts with him. She refused and was able to leave.

However, a few weeks later an older male actor invited her to his home under the guise that he would help her progress with her career. Instead he assaulted her, she wrote in her book.

The predatory actor has since died.

The comedy star, known for shows including Goodness Gracious Me and The Kumars at No 42, did not report the incidents to the police and did not tell family or friends as it "was the culture" of the industry at the time.

She recalled: "When I have talked about this incident to other women, particularly of my age, they've all said that happened to me and a lot of them have never talked about it because it was part of the culture.

"The 70s, 80s and 90s, it was absolutely part of the culture.

"You wouldn't even bother to report half of these things because A, you wouldn't be believed and B, everyone was doing it."

Joining the BBC in the 1990s, she rose to prominence as part of the team behind the broadcaster's sketch comedy, Goodness Gracious Me!

In 1993, she wrote the screenplay for the comedy-drama film Bhaji On The Beach, and two years later she starred in the Channel 4 romantic comedy film, Beautiful Thing.

The award-winner was a key writer and actress on the 1996 show, and later helped to bring Bollywood to the West End, by co-writing Andrew Lloyd Webber's Bombay Dreams in 2002.

You can listen to the full interview with Dame Meera Syal on Asian Network Trending on BBC Sounds.

If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.

EntertainmentTab.title: Aardman at 50: Gromit was nearly a cat, Shaun the Sheep almost spoke
EntertainmentTab.text:
Gromit was almost a cat. Shaun the Sheep was nearly given a voice. And Chicken Run helped change the Oscars forever.

As Aardman Animations marks its 50th birthday, its creators have been sharing some of the surprising twists behind the rise of Bristol's best-known creative success story.

Founded by school friends Sir Peter Lord and Sir David Sproxton in 1976, Aardman has given us Morph, Wallace and Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run, the world's most successful stop-motion film.

But the journey from two teenagers "mucking about with plasticine" to an Oscar-winning animation powerhouse has often hinged on chance decisions, practical compromises and creative instinct.

Few examples are better than Gromit.

Wallace and Gromit became Aardman's most famous characters after animator Nick Park joined the studio in 1985.

But Gromit was not always a dog.

"I had this idea of an English guy who builds a rocket, in the basement of his house," recalled Park.

"I was thinking he may have a pet, probably a cat."

The switch was surprisingly simple.

"I started modelling the cat, and it was just very difficult, so I thought I'd do a dog instead!"

Park was developing A Grand Day Out at the National Film and Television School in London when Lord and Sproxton came to speak to students.

"We met him and thought, 'Oh, he's good'. In fact, he's very good. Now I know him, he's actually a genius," said Lord.

The combination was electric. A Grand Day Out was nominated for an Oscar in 1990, losing only to another Aardman production, Creature Comforts, also directed by Park.

Pointing to a poster of Wallace and Gromit floating over Bristol in a hot-air balloon, Lord reflected on their appeal.

"When they appear on the screen, you laugh before they do anything."

Park later won three more Oscars. Perhaps it was just as well he never mastered Gromit the Cat.

By the mid-1990s, Wallace and Gromit had made Aardman one of the most talked-about names in animation.

That success led to an unlikely meeting with Steven Spielberg.

At dinner with Spielberg and DreamWorks chief executive Jeffrey Katzenberg, they pitched what became Chicken Run.

"We want to do The Great Escape," Lord told Spielberg.

"But with chickens."

"I had always been a fan of Aardman," Katzenberg said. "And I had this secret ambition that someday there would be a way to work together."

Park remembered Spielberg's response.

"Spielberg said, 'The Great Escape is one of my favourite films, and I have 300 chickens on my ranch!' So it went very well."

No-one had ever made a 90-minute stop-motion feature from modelling clay. The budget was more than £20m, and Aardman insisted every frame would be shot in Bristol.

The gamble paid off. Chicken Run took more than $220m (£165m) worldwide and remains the highest-grossing stop-motion film ever made.

But it did not win an Oscar.

At the time there was no Academy Award for animated features.

"And so because they couldn't give Chicken Run a little golden man, they invented the category," said Radio 1 film critic Ali Plumb.

The Academy introduced the Best Animated Feature Oscar the following year.

"And a couple of years later, Wallace and Gromit won that Oscar for 'The Curse of the Were-Rabbit', so they got their own reward," Plumb said.

If Chicken Run proved Aardman could conquer Hollywood, another character would go on to conquer the world.

Shaun first appeared in the Wallace and Gromit film A Close Shave in 1995 and has become one of the studio's biggest global stars.

Like all the other animals, he expresses himself through bleats, grunts and hugely dynamic facial expressions.

"The beauty of Shaun is it transcends borders and cultures because it doesn't rely on the spoken word," said Aardman's Managing Director Sean Clarke.

"You can literally see Shaun the Sheep here in Bristol and in Outer Mongolia."

Yet executives repeatedly urged Aardman to give him a voice.

"When we launched the Shaun the Sheep series, we were told to add voices," Clarke remembered.

The same argument resurfaced when Shaun got his own feature film in 2015.

"They said, 'You can't do 80 minutes without any dialogue'.

"But we stuck to our convictions, and I think it is now one of our most revered films."

Lord insists Shaun was not kept silent to boost international sales, it simply "seemed better that way".

However, the character's global appeal is undeniable. Clarke said Shaun has been sold into 170 countries and is especially popular in Asia.

"Shaun is actually our most valuable character now.

"Wallace and Gromit built the house, but Shaun keeps the lights on."

If that cheque gave them a company name, their next creation gave them a star.

Lord and Sproxton moved to Bristol to work on Take Hart, the successor to Vision On.

On this show they took what Lord called "a leap into the third dimension".

"Plasticine was cheap", Lord explained.

"The budgets were low, and you can work quickly with it."

Soon he had fashioned Morph, the simple little terracotta brown figure that can change shape into anything, hence his name.

"It was just so easy to squash him up and reform him as a dog, or a submarine, or a bird or anything," Lord said.

Morph became a hit with children and parents alike, and remains a fixture at Aardman's Bristol headquarters.

Back in 1989, Lord told a BBC West documentary The Animators he "hoped Morph will still be around in 30 years or so, and still be loved."

It has been 37 years since he said that, and an Aardman exhibition at Bristol's MShed Museum was recently packed with Morph superfans.

But Lord, now the studio's creative director, still comes into the office and playfully reshapes Morph while chatting.

I asked him what Wallace would make of it all.

"Oh, he'd probably just say 'Cracking careers lads!'" he smiled.

EntertainmentTab.title: Why Northern Ireland was the 'perfect place' for The Death of Robin Hood
EntertainmentTab.text:
It is a centuries old legend of stealing from the rich to give to the poor, freshly adapted for the big screen, filmed entirely in Northern Ireland.

The Death of Robin Hood is based on a 17th Century ballad of the outlaw, starring Hugh Jackman as the reflective, battle-weary titular character at the end of his life. It presents a darker, less family-friendly version of the medieval hero.

A Belfast actress, who played a small role in the film, told BBC News NI about sharing the screen with A-listers and why Northern Ireland was now "the perfect place" to make a film.

Tabitha Smyth, from the east of the city, was cast as Sarah in her first role in a major studio feature film.

"The film's set in England, but Northern Ireland is just like the perfect place to film for everyone at the minute - you can get from a beach to a city centre, to a forest park, all within 20 minutes of each other," Smyth said.

"It's like a dream for a production like this, where it is set hundreds of years ago, hence why Game of Thrones and stuff like How to Train Your Dragon etc have all been filmed in the north."

Filming spanned across a wide range of picturesque parts of the country including Silent Valley, Glenarm and Murlough Bay.

Production was also based at Belfast Harbour Studios, whilst the film's post-production process was completed at the company Yellow Moon in Holywood.

The film has a small cast but some big names - Jodie Comer, Bill Skarsgård and Noah Jupe.

Smyth said it was "very daunting", but Comer and Jackman were "so down to earth"

"Obviously going into a film like that when you haven't been in a film before and then you're just like on set with like Jodie Comer and Hugh Jackman," she said.

"It was pretty much every scene or every part I was doing they were in there as well, which was kind of mad."

Strangford and Bushmills were also among the locations to provide a dramatic backdrop for the film.

"There were times where mad storms were happening, when they were filming, like it was kind of crazy, rain, hail and snow," Smyth said.

The actor said filming in Northern Ireland brought an authenticity to the film.

"We were filming a scene and it was absolutely freezing, like on the edge of a cliff. There was a fire lit and the wind was mad, but it just adds to it because it would have looked look like that," she said.

Northern Ireland is also popular with the crews, she added.

"The people are all really sound, the food's good, the craic is good and people are really drawn to it at the minute in producing work here," she said.

"Game of Thrones has a really big part to play in that for sure."

Andrew Reid, chief content officer at Northern Ireland Screen, told BBC News NI that productions like this have become a "regular occurrence" in Northern Ireland.

He said there had been a particular rise in the number of indigenous productions – that is, productions written, directed and produced in Northern Ireland.

Like Smyth, he believes Northern Ireland lends itself perfectly to film-making.

"We are a small but very compact region, it's easy to get around," Reid said.

"Time on the road is wasted money.

"We can be up a mountain in the morning, and in a studio in the afternoon. There's a really good selection of diverse locations."

However, Reid said Northern Ireland had other star qualities for film-makers.

"We have a fantastic ecosystem that has been built up over decades," he said. "We have fantastic people.

"We also have a very strong training remit within our productions that we're building up those crews."

Reid added that the region's "state-of-the-art facilities" were also a major draw.

So how long until Northern Ireland can call itself a major player in European film?

According to Reid, the talent, facilities and landscape of the area mean it might be sooner than some expect.

"We're starting to see the beginning of it already."

The Death of Robin Hood was released in the UK on 2 September.

EntertainmentTab.title: Carla Jeffery: 'Beautiful, vibrant' Disney star dies aged 33
EntertainmentTab.text:
US actress Carla Jeffery, who was known for appearing in 2018 Disney Channel movie Zombies and two sequels, has died at the age of 33.

Announcing the news, her agent Carla Alexander described her as a "beautiful, vibrant and incredibly talented woman whose radiant smile could light up any room".

Jeffery played cheerleader Bree in Zombies and its follow-ups in 2020 and 2022, and previously had a recurring role in Curb Your Enthusiasm as one of the Black family, who moved in with Larry David after Hurricane Katrina.

No cause of death has been given.

Her management company Alexanders Talent wrote on Instagram, external: "Our hearts are broken as we mourn the loss of our beloved Carla Jeffery.

"For more than 20 years, Carla was part of the Alexanders Talent Management family and watching her grow from a talented young girl into the beautiful, vibrant woman and actress she became was an incredible privilege.

"We will remember her infectious smile, her laughter, her talent, and the beautiful light she carried everywhere she went.

"Our deepest love and condolences are with Carla's family and loved ones. We ask that their privacy be respected during this incredibly difficult time. Rest beautifully, Carla. You will be deeply missed and forever loved."

Jeffery's twin brother Carlon, who is also an actor, reposted that statement as well as a clip of his sister on a beach and a screenshot of an undated text message.

"Hey Sis, call me back when you get this. I was just calling to see how your day went! I love you to the moon & back sis," it read.

"I just want you to know how proud I am of you. Your resilience, your grace, your infectious smile that lights up a room. You are truly a light that shines bright. Don't let anyone dim that light, even yourself.

"The light you carry is special and must be protected at all times. You are the best sister a brother could ask for. Pray we continue to grow closer to one another along this journey. I got your back in this life and the next."

Her co-stars also paid tribute, with Chandler Kinney, who played Willa in Zombies, writing that the actress's death "doesn't feel real".

"Carla. The sweetest, most sparkly gal. You made every day better and brighter with your infectious positivity," Kinney wrote.

"I think part of why you brought such effervescence to Bree (aside from your immense talent) is because that's really who you were in your heart; a bubbly, vivacious heart-of-gold cheerleader who loved nothing more than to uplift those around her."

Milo Manheim, who played Zed, shared a series of photos with the caption: "Love you Carlaboo, the sweetest, kindest, most loving person."

EntertainmentTab.title: Dame Prue Leith: 'When you're old, you don't give a toss'
EntertainmentTab.text:
"When you're old, you don't give a toss what anyone thinks, really, so you feel very free. You can have a snooze in the afternoon, and nobody thinks that's odd."

Dame Prue Leith is celebrating her perceived joys of the golden years as she prepares to discuss "Growing Old Disgracefully" with fellow authors Gyles Brandreth and Kathy Lette.

The trio will take to the stage at this year's Cheltenham Literature Festival on 15 October to prove to the audience ageing is "not the dreaded thing" it is made out to be, the former Bake Off judge said.

Dame Prue said: "You come into your own, you don't care what people think, you're not going to change. And so the world has to just put up with it."

At 86, the restaurateur and cookery writer has reflected on her younger years and has decided that growing old is good fun, although she acknowledged it may be different for those who are "old and lonely and ill".

"When I think of my teenage years, I think they were really stressful," Dame Prue said.

"I was always bringing the wrong boys home, and I was quarrelling with my parents, and I didn't know what I wanted to do.

"I was sort of lost and didn't believe in myself at all... I wanted a boyfriend, couldn't get one, you know. Old age is unstressful."

EntertainmentTab.title: Steve Irwin's family celebrates 'superhero' dad, 20 years after shock death
EntertainmentTab.text:
Australian conservationist Bindi Irwin has marked the 20th anniversary of her famous father's death with a touching tribute to the man best known as the "Crocodile Hunter".

Steve Irwin died on 4 September 2006, aged 44, after a stingray fatally pierced his chest while he was underwater filming a documentary at the Great Barrier Reef.

Bindi, who was eight when her father died, called Steve a "superhero" in an online post on Friday, saying she has "watched the world mourn my dad with our family" for the past two decades.

"I always thought that my dad's legacy is wildlife conservation; it turns out, his legacy is love. For our planet and for each other," Bindi, 28, wrote on Instagram.

She described the impact of her father's death on her mother Terri and her younger brother Robert, 22.

"My mum lost the love of her life; my brother and I lost the greatest dad," she wrote. "Grief never truly leaves us; we walk alongside it every day."

Bindi also shared details on how her daughter connects with the grandfather she never got to meet.

"I have a 5-year-old daughter who watches his documentaries every morning. She feels utterly loved by her 'grandpa crocodile' without ever having met him."

Since Steve's death, the Irwins have continued to run Australia Zoo in Queensland.

"My dad left a lasting impact so poignant that it will ripple out for generations to come," Bindi wrote, saying his life and legacy were "worth celebrating".

She thanked Steve for being the family's "guardian angel" and signed off her message saying she loved him "with my whole heart".

Steve's wife Terri also took to social media to mark the day, posting an interview where the khaki-clad wildlife advocate recounted Bindi's birth and its impact on him.

"The most incredible wildlife encounter of my life was the birth of my daughter, Bindi," Steve says in the interview, with his signature enthusiasm.

The first time he held his newborn child, the inspiration for her name hit him.

"I was flabbergasted and it was then that her name evolved. I've gone, 'Bindi!' after my favourite crocodile, Bindi," he said, with a wide grin.

Robert Irwin also posted a tribute to his father, with a photo of Steve holding him when he was a baby, alongside the caption, "Your legacy is forever".

Last November, Robert was crowned the winner of US dance competition Dancing with the Stars, a decade after his sister won the same title.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘I didn’t know if I’d ever have sex again’: inside Sharon Horgan’s excruciating post-divorce comedy
EntertainmentTab.text:
When Sharon Horgan walked into HBO to pitch her new series, Youth, she basically just said “sandwich generation” to them. Alex, the protagonist, is squished between a teenage son and two elderly parents. That’s the classic; the rest of it – the recent divorce, the dating hell, the busy, creative professional life full of pricks – is the icing on the sandwich (if you like). Horgan had been incubating some of the characters for five years, but “honestly”, she tells me, “I said about three sentences and a week later, they said yes. I’ve never had that experience before.”

You might think you can imagine it, but Youth is unlike any portrait you’ve ever seen in the gallery of (for brevity) menopausal women doing everything for everyone. There’s an urgency and valour to it that is very much drawn from Horgan’s own experience. “Everything just changed for me when I hit my 50s,” she says. “I was very bamboozled but I really had a hunger to make time count.” Not every situation is lifted directly from her own life, post-divorce – she’s also borrowing from her friends, she emphasises – but in general terms, the pressures, the worries, the outrages, the surprise and the delight are all so exquisitely drawn that even if it’s not Horgan herself, you hope someone, somewhere, is living this in real life.

I caught some of the shooting on a blowy day in April this year, in east London. Horgan and her co-star Rupert Friend were filming a crux scene. Friend plays Patrick, slightly younger than Horgan’s Alex, a little indecisive and shambling. “He’s not a Prince Charming character. I don’t think I’m the answer to all her ills,” he says, walking around a little park in between takes. Patrick wants to be with Alex, but he also thinks he wants children and there’s no way she’s going back there again, even if she could. “Sharon flips the proverbial biological clock on its head,” he says. “Men think it doesn’t apply to them because they ostensibly can make children all the way through. He’s never considered that it’s not his clock.”

Nothing passes between Alex and Patrick that’s overstated or even out of the ordinary, unless you count the fact that she gets hit by a cyclist as she walks away. But when it slots into the finished show, it is, like every other scene, hilarious. I just do not know how Horgan does what she does – which is what every one of her co-stars says about her. “She could have chemistry with a toaster,” says Aran Murphy (yes, son of Cillian), who plays her son. “She’s so fizzing with energy.” Rupert Friend puts the emphasis on her agility: “Sharon’s just brilliant at writing. She’s able to do that dance between jokes and pathos in a way that I don’t know anyone else can do.” But it’s Horgan herself who, in an absolutely unboastful way, explains it best: “I’m allergic to sentimentality. I can’t abide anything that is sweet or schmaltzy. But I love genuine emotion. I love to make people feel things. As much as I love the laughs, I’d feel like I’d failed in some way if I wasn’t giving people pain.”

Murphy’s Ruari is a gift of a part, the most believably wrecking-ball 18-year-old son you’ve ever seen. Some things he wrecks on purpose (the last day of secondary school), some he wrecks by accident (his first week at university; his life), but the stakes are agonisingly high and the actions all plausible. Horgan has a lot to say about parenting kids this age, “even though I do not have a son, I have daughters” (Sadhbh, 22, and Amer, 18). “Gen Z have that awful feeling of being the last generation. They’re here at a point in time where they’re being told that everything’s fucked and AI’s going to take your jobs. I sometimes don’t know how to get out of bed in the morning, but they’re the ones who care the most and feel things the most.”

Murphy is pretty reserved in real life (he speaks to me by Zoom from Italy, where he is on holiday), and the performance he turns in is one of the most thrillingly angry teenagers ever. “We really got lucky with Aran,” says Horgan. “There’s nothing about him that isn’t real. It made life so much easier to be working with someone who you literally can’t see acting.” She wanted Ruari to be “complex but not in a Dawson’s Creek way – a real boy who’s a little bit broken. All Alex wants is for him to normalise. But what’s normal?”

Besides, Ruari is probably saying the same about his mother, who he is furious to discover still has gentleman callers. Patrick isn’t Alex’s only love interest; there’s also a sex scene with Tim McInnerny (Percy from Blackadder) that I am still laughing at weeks later. None of the relationships, fleeting or otherwise, are at all a classic love story – Rupert Friend says ruefully, “I’m really the best of a bad bunch, which I am happy to take as the quote for my gravestone” – but the men are drawn so truthfully that you can’t help but love them all slightly (apart from the ex-husband, and even he’s not a bad guy, more of an emotional no-mark).

“When I found myself divorced,” Horgan says, “I genuinely thought I’d be alone for ever. I didn’t even know if I’d ever have sex again. There’s that extreme fear of being alone and being lonely. But at the same time, you think you have a freedom as well. You do suddenly think: ‘My kids have finished school, I’ve got some time to try and get this right.’” Alex’s love life is anything but over, yet this isn’t a “you go, girl” tale where every woman remains perpetually 35 through Botox and force of will. “You put yourself out there in a slightly different way,” says Horgan. “It’s still incredibly difficult, as a woman of that age, to find someone – the men who are left are either institutionally single or they’re divorced or they’re looking for someone much younger.”

The subplot of Alex’s ageing parents, meanwhile, is so honest it’s exhilarating. Dramedy tends to be respectfully saccharine about the elderly, and skate over the inconvenient bits: the stubbornness, the denial, the endless hospital appointments. But (I’m allowed to say this, being an orphan – Horgan’s mother is still alive, her dad died in 2023), those bits are almost the whole of the experience. “There is a huge amount of non-cooperation there,” she says, “and why shouldn’t there be? Ageing is hard. It’s harder when it begins to affect you mentally. When you’ve always been sharp as a tack, or when you begin to lose your mobility and you’ve always been a fucking go-getter. Losing those basic functions is brutal.”

But from Alex’s point of view, “all the planning, all the phone calls, it becomes such a huge part of your life. As it goes on, you’ll see how it affects her sibling relationship as well. I wanted to explore that all so much but you run out of time and space. That could have been a whole show.”

Alex works in publishing, and there are some fabulous performances by her authors – Anne Reid, as a grande dame of airport fiction, turning her hand to erotica, alongside Harriet Walter as her ice-cold daughter. “I could talk to you about Anne Reid for the entirety of the interview,” Horgan says. “It’s hard to even mention her and not just wax lyrical about being aged 91 and still delivering work on that level and still caring so much.” Damian Lewis, within 30 seconds of arriving on screen, has distilled everything that is bad about publishing, celebrity, London, private members’ clubs and the world. “Everyone who came on to do their bits was influencing the show,” says Horgan. “I was writing it at the same time as making it, which was hell.” On the upside, it meant she was building relationships with her co-stars as she wrote, and incorporating those connections. Friend remembers deep conversations about what love actually is. “We talked about how heartbreaking it is to think about things in terms of if they fail. You know, if you meet and immediately think: ‘We could date, but if we date we might break up.’ Why do anything? Everything has a pessimistic possibility, and Alex is always considering it, but it’s no way to live.”

Pulling, Sharon Horgan’s 00s comedy, and Motherland, a decade ago, did the same thing – which is to say, if you’d asked: “Do you want to see a show about three single women? How about a school-gate show about neurotic middle-class people and Chardonnay and mini Babybels?” I’d have said: “No, not at all, sounds drab and also too close to home.” But then when they landed, they were all I wanted to watch. Youth is technically about the grinding sandwich years, when everything gets harder at once, and then your joints stop working. But it’s really about the sheer bliss of being alive when so much happens that is funny, stitched together by a fearsomely long to-do list.

Youth is on HBO Max from 21 September.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘Men calling us woke need our show more than most’: punks Piss on finding strength in visceral confrontations of sexual violence
EntertainmentTab.text:
You’d be hard pressed to find a band with fewer airs and graces than Piss. First, there’s the unavoidable matter of their name, which they style in all caps, no nonsense; a word that scans as vulgar and combative but also somewhat facetious when displayed on their merch in loopy cursive, sometimes decorated with bows. The Vancouver quartet’s music is a merciless cyclone of hardcore, poetry, sound collage and performance art that revolves entirely around singer Taylor Zantingh’s experiences with sexual violence.

On stage at Eindhoven’s Hit the City festival in late August, the band greets the stacked crowd with a trigger warning before drummer Garreth Roberts, bassist Gavin Moya and guitarist Tyler Paterson launch into pulverising fits of noise-punk, broken up by audio samples of children laughing and feminist writer Andrea Dworkin talking about pornography. Zantingh hurls herself around, clutching at her stomach and flinging her pigtails before winding down to a nervous, twitching standstill. The intense set is finely tuned to present a narrative of gender-based violence not as entertainment, but as lived experience. They play it exactly the same every night, and have done for the last two years.

“I think a lot of people are like, ‘I’m going to see a band called Piss, this is going to be craaaazy!’ And it’s crazy in a different way than they expect,” Zantingh tells me before the show, over chamomile tea. “People come for one thing and then they’re forced to listen to me for half an hour.”

The buzz around Piss usually takes bands of their ilk several album cycles to drum up, yet they have released next to no music: a four-track demo on Bandcamp, a few professionally recorded sets and radio appearances on YouTube and some viral fan-filmed clips. Since forming in 2024, their reputation has grown through their live performance, prompting Sub Pop to sign them; their debut album You Made Me / Skin on Linen arrives in October.

Recorded over a handful of days in winter 2024, the album was made to mirror the Piss live experience as closely as possible. Throughout, you’ll hear Zantingh gasp for breath or struggle to get words out, lacing traumatic recollections with disturbing imagery of “fingers sewn in the wrong places” and kids “practising blowjobs on glue sticks”. The songs combine Bikini Kill and Fugazi’s DIY approach to “making personal things political” with the uranium-heavy sonics of Chat Pile or Swans. Paterson, who is primarily responsible for shaping the instrumentals, likens his process to scoring a film. “The influences came from a lot of places to uphold the narrative that Tay is weaving,” he says. “The feelings and intention come first, and the sound comes after.”

The way Piss use music, performance art and other voices is fundamental, Zantingh says, because the subject matter is too “monstrous” to be described in words alone. Placing her voice in chorus with a range of others – activists, philosophers, militants, psychoanalysts and transgressive literary figures, including French philosopher Manon Garcia speaking about the trial of Gisèle Pelicot – leaves things open to interpretation. “One reason I feel so strong when I’m on stage is because I’ve found the right way to communicate it, versus trying to confess these things in a literal sense. When I’m telling [the audience] how these events still hurt me today, and they’re watching me hurt myself in real time, they’re watching that injury in a very tangible way.”

While Piss try to provide as many access points to their music as possible, it is, at every level, deeply uncomfortable. When I describe their twisted instrumentals as “gross”, drummer Garreth Roberts says, “That’s Ty’s [guitarist Tyler Paterson] favourite word!” Zantingh’s voice jolts unpredictably from soft spoken-word to chainsaw shriek. All lyrics and samples (which they consider a reading list) are also prominently subtitled in their videos, for accessibility and so the subject matter doesn’t take a backseat to the visuals. “I’d like to be able to print them out so people can have them at the shows – almost like a little programme, like when you go to church,” says Zantingh.

In the queue before the gig, a number of men were sniggering about the name Piss. I wonder whether the band feel their music is always met on its own terms. Zantingh recalls seeing two older men at the front of a festival set. “When I was doing the trigger warning they were like, ‘Woke!’ and then walked off,” she says with a weary smile. “The irony is they probably need that show more than most people there, but I accepted early on that the people I want to play the set for might not be the people I can have the most impact on.”

On the precipice of a debut album release through one of the most revered independent labels, Piss find themselves contemplating an uncertain future. “Part of the reason we waited so long to release the record is because I don’t know, and I have never known, how long I’m gonna be able to physically and emotionally do this,” Zantingh states plainly. “I spend my life trying to turn my pain into something beautiful,” she screams on I Wanted to Be a Singer.

“The foundation of Piss is built on my suffering,” she continues. “We literally cannot exist the way that we exist if you remove that.” That might be unsustainable in the long run, but for now, she says, “it’s exactly what it’s supposed to be”.

You Made Me / Skin on Linen is released via Sub Pop on 30 October. Piss are at Brighton Psych fest on 4 September, End of the Road on 6 September and then tour North America and Europe

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘Like a tired boxer, battered by applause’: as Andrew Scott’s biopic premieres, Richard Eyre remembers Ian Charleson’s superb, near-death Hamlet
EntertainmentTab.text:
Ian Charleson was one of the finest actors of his generation and an important figure in the fight for gay rights. Yet the extraordinary circumstances of his final performance as Hamlet, just months before his death, are less familiar.

Now, a new film is bringing that haunting production back to life. Elsinore, directed by Simon Stone and starring Andrew Scott as the Scottish actor, will premiere at Telluride this weekend before opening the London film festival in October.

Charleson was 40 and terminally ill with Aids when he was cast as Hamlet in Richard Eyre’s 1989 production at the National Theatre, after Daniel Day-Lewis abruptly left the role. Charleson had first played Hamlet 15 years earlier and persuaded Eyre to let him reprise it, despite the director’s misgivings about his health.

“Ian was very bright, very witty, mischievous,” Eyre told the Guardian. “He was beyond good-looking. He was beautiful, and he had a beautiful singing voice.”

Eyre remembered sitting with Charleson in the National’s canteen a year earlier, when the actor was starring in Cat on a Hot Tin Roof. “He said, ‘I’m hungry for the big Shakespeare roles’. So when Dan had his breakdown” – Day-Lewis believed he saw the ghost of his father onstage – “I thought, I will approach Ian. We met, and then I realised Ian was was very ill. But I thought I will go with him anyway.”

The cast, crew, and audience were told that Charleson’s face was swollen after a sinus operation. In reality, he was suffering from septicaemia, enduring painful acupuncture during rehearsals and, later, chemotherapy.

“Ian’s beautiful face was actually deformed by the disease,” Eyre said. “But I just thought, he is determined, and I felt determined, and it was sort of an act of love for a friend. Most people told me I was absolutely insane. The press were characteristically loathsome in their probing. I just stubbornly stuck to my decision. In retrospect, it was the right one. He was heroic, and utterly brilliant in the part.”

The production ran for six weeks and was widely regarded as one of the finest Hamlets seen on stage. The day after Charleson’s last show, Ian McKellen refused the Evening Standard award for best actor and gave his statuette to Charleson instead.

Charleson died on 6 January 1990, eight weeks later, having asked that Aids be recorded as the cause – an unusually public act at a time when the disease was feared and stigmatised.

Eyre has written of how fitting it was for Charleson to play Hamlet in the last months of his life. “Do you think I can go on as Hamlet looking like this?” Charleson asked him. “You’ll get better,” Eyre replied. “We have to be positive,” Charleson said.

“Hamlet is a poem of death,” Eyre wrote. “It charts one of the great human rites of passage – from immaturity to accommodation with death. Hamlet grows up, in effect, to grow dead.”

Born in Edinburgh in 1949, Charleson trained at the Bristol Old Vic. He played Eric Liddell in Chariots of Fire, which won four Oscars including best picture, and also appeared in the following year’s best picture winner, Richard Attenborough’s Gandhi.

Charleson seemed to have all the ingredients of a major film career: he was handsome, charismatic and intelligent, with a formidable technical ability. Yet his film career never took off as expected. Instead, he repeatedly returned to the stage, performing Shakespeare, Tennessee Williams, Chekhov, Sam Shepard.

Michael Billington, the Guardian’s former chief theatre critic, remembers Charleson as Eddie in Shepard’s Fool for Love at the Cottesloe in 1984. Initially unconvinced by his interpretation, Billington later came to remember the performance for its “mixture of masculinity and sensitivity”. Charleson performed Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, he said, with “the same blend of supposedly contradictory qualities: athleticism and delicacy”.

Charleson was gay at a time when being openly so could damage an actor’s career. Diagnosed with HIV in 1986, he took part in Before the Act, McKellen’s 1988 anti-Section 28 gala, alongside Judi Dench, Vanessa Redgrave and Stephen Fry.

Scott, who played Hamlet 150 times in London in 2017, has found himself returning to the role while portraying the actor who performed it at the end of his life.

“The idea that Ian was doing this when he was so sick is still, to my mind, just completely mind-blowing,” Scott told People. “And his decision to do it was just incredibly courageous.”

Scott said he was moved by “the opportunity to play a part that Ian and his contemporaries would not have gotten while they were working actors.”

He added: “I wanted people to be able to understand that he was trying to live – it’s not about fetishising his death. He was so full of life and fun, and he did this extraordinary thing.”

Critics and industry insiders are heavily tipping Scott for a best actor Oscar nomination following early praise for his performance. Eyre called it “brilliant”. “He looks like Ian, and he touches the heart like Ian,” he said.

Charleson’s most celebrated performance was never preserved on film. What remains are recollections, photographs and accounts of an actor performing with extraordinary intensity while his body failed him.

Eyre recalled that Charleson had flu and missed two nights, but felt guilty: “If they pay you, you should turn up.” His final, Monday night performance, Eyre wrote, was “like watching a man who had been rehearsing for playing Hamlet all his life. He wasn’t playing the part, he became it.”

At the curtain call, Charleson stood “like a tired boxer, battered by applause”.

A few weeks before he died, just before Christmas, he wrote to Eyre: “One day when I’m better I’d love to attempt Hamlet again, and all the rest; and together we can revitalise Shakespeare. Anyway I hope this is not a dream and I can’t tell you how much of a kick I got out of doing the part, if only for the short time I could …”

EntertainmentTab.title: Queer Edward II review – funny, touching time capsule of Derek Jarman at work
EntertainmentTab.text:
There could hardly be a more vivid time-capsule film about the publicly funded British arts scene in the early 1990s than this engrossing fly-on-the-wall documentary about Derek Jarman and his movie Edward II. Based on the play by Christopher Marlowe, it is about the 14th-century English king and his love affair with his court favourite, Piers Gaveston, with Steven Waddington and Andrew Tiernan as the leads and Tilda Swinton as Queen Isabella.

This film uses the tremendously funny and candid making-of footage shot at the time by Seamus McGarvey, who had worked as a camera assistant on earlier Jarman films War Requiem and The Garden, and whose distinguished career as a cinematographer lay ahead. Jarman emerges as an effortless leader with a beaming patrician authority, rather like David Lean or Richard Attenborough, the kind of chief whom subordinates instinctively wish to please while keeping from him the grubby problems that they themselves have to deal with, such as paying quarrelsome extras or handling tabloid press questions. Jarman had had his HIV diagnosis for five years at this stage, managing the situation with meds which McGarvey’s camera notices.

Jarman’s tightly budgeted movie was composed in the formalised theatrical setpiece style that Peter Greenaway favoured in the same period; he intended a radically confrontational piece of Brechtian queer cinema, reinventing the Marlowe play as a movie insurgency against homophobia, Section 28, the (declining but still present) indifference to HIV/Aids research, and age-of-consent inequality. Jarman used Peter Tatchell’s OutRage! protesters as extras in the movie studio, effectively making the film and the street protests part and parcel of each other. This was to lead to one of the most bizarre and chaotic footnotes in British movie history, amusingly shown here in all its uproarious craziness: the OutRage! shock troops stormed into the studios next door where Cliff Richard happened to be rehearsing, demanding that he out himself.

The “outing” debate now in fact looks very dated and this is the one moment where you can sense that Jarman thinks that the OutRage! protesters got it wrong by harassing and bullying Cliff Richard; we see him assuring his own team later that Tatchell gave them a real telling off for this. (Did Tatchell actually do anything of the kind? Or is that what Jarman felt ought to have happened?) It’s an absorbing and affecting portrait of a dedicated artist at work.

GeneralTab.title: Nigel Farage unveils small boats deal with Jordan Bardella at Reform conference
GeneralTab.text:
Nigel Farage has agreed a deal with France's hard-right National Rally (RN) party on returning migrants who attempt to cross the English Channel in small boats, should both parties win power.

It comes after Reform UK last month announced a plan to intercept boats and return migrants to French ports using the Royal Navy.

The proposed agreement with RN states that France would "ordinarily accept" those on board, and then repatriate them to their home country.

It was signed at Reform's annual conference in Birmingham by RN President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of presidential elections in April next year.

In a speech in the main conference hall, ahead of the deal being unveiled, Bardella told delegates that an RN government would "do everything in its power to ensure that France is no longer the gateway for illegal migration into the United Kingdom".

Hailing Farage as the UK's next prime minister, Bardella pledged to work with a potential future Reform government to tackle illegal migration.

The "memorandum of understanding" unveiled at the conference is a political document, but could be developed into a legal agreement between two future governments, if both parties win power.

It states: "The United Kingdom will intercept boats which have launched from French shores and entered British territorial waters and will return the persons on board to France.

"France will ordinarily accept these persons, who will be repatriated to their home country in accordance with the law in force in France concerning expulsion."

Under the proposals, illegal migrants who successfully arrive in the UK from France would be immediately detained and deported to their home country, rather than to France, under plans previously outlined by Reform.

Challenged during a news conference over whether the wording "ordinarily" meant some migrants would not be accepted by France, Farage said it was "legalese".

He argued the proposals would mean there was "no incentive" to pay a trafficker to cross the Channel, and "in very, very short order the business model is broken".

Farage said the "historic document" would "stop the boats forever".

Achieving this goal within the first 100 days of a Reform government is one of the party's key pledges.

Last month Emmanuel Macron's government hit out at Reform's proposals to use the Navy to return migrant boats to France, saying the they would violate the country's sovereignty and breach international law.

Opposition parties also branded the plan unworkable.

Labour has pointed to increased cooperation with France as contributing to the number of small boat crossings falling.

This includes extra officers being deployed to French beaches, and more funding to help prevent crossings.

Last year Sir Keir Starmer's government also signed a "one in, one out deal", which allows the UK to send some small boat-arrivals back to France, while agreeing to take the same number of people from France believed to have a legitimate claim to come to the UK.

GeneralTab.title: Falkland Islands: UK support 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims
GeneralTab.text:
The UK's position on the Falkland Islands is "unwavering", Downing Street has said after Argentina's president said the islands were "historically and legally" Argentinian.

Andy Burnham "fully supports the wishes of the islanders to remain a British overseas territory", a Downing Street spokesperson said.

Javier Milei said the "winds of change" favoured his country's claim to the islands and pledged sanctions on firms planning to exploit oil close to the islands.

A British and Israeli partnership due to begin exploration work on the Sea Lion oilfield said it didn't expect recent developments to affect its work in the region.

More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Britain and Argentina.

However in a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

When asked about if the prime minister believed the UK had the necessary forces to defend the sovereignty of the islands the spokesperson said "they will remain so far as long as the islanders wish".

"Our armed forces are on standby 24/7 to protect the UK and our interests", the spokesperson added.

Announcing his plan for sanctions in a national address on Thursday, Milei reiterated that the Falkland Islands were "historically and legally" Argentinian.

He said: "There can be no argument. They are part of the Argentine territory.

"The islanders on their usurped territory do not have a legitimate right to self-determination and any argument on any such self-determination is invalid."

Milei described the Sea Lion oilfield as a "clear and present danger", and said if Argentina does not act swiftly, "they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea – something that has never happened before."

He continued: "The Falklands are our future, we need to recover these islands which are nationally relevant. There is no other path forward".

It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.

A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government."

The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".

Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas.

"That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline".

On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.

Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review.

On Friday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the islands.

Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders."

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable".

"Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.

In an earlier statement, Downing Street said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands.

GeneralTab.title: How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views
GeneralTab.text:
The prospect of an imminent agreement to end the conflict between the US and Iran again seems unlikely, with the warring sides exchanging strikes and uncompromising rhetoric.

The attacks come days after the US said it was moving into a new phase - a sweeping economic blockade against Iran and countries which trade with it.

The US aim was to force Iran to negotiate and to stop its attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The key commercial shipping route has been effectively closed since the US and Israel started the conflict in February.

A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) the two sides signed in June and meant to result in a permanent ceasefire and a deal within 60 days has expired.

As the conflict enters its seventh month, we asked three experts for their thoughts on how it may play out.

Jason Campbell, Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DC

The problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic objectives are in Iran. The White House is persistently re-evaluating what it is willing to live with from a political standpoint.

It was assumed the military component would be enough for a quick victory and that has not had the desired effect.

What we are seeing is different levers - both military and economic - that the US is trying to pull at.

Right now, the administration appears satisfied with some form of stasis. I think they are satisfied with maintaining the blockade and with allowing some periodic targeting against Iran's capability to upset the shipping lane in the strait.

US officials are hopeful that the new sanctions will be enough to compel the Iranian regime to come to the negotiating table in a weaker position.

US forces have seemingly been able to facilitate a sufficient trickle through the Strait of Hormuz in recent days to avert an oil-price shock or a global economic collapse. But those were not the US objectives when starting the war.

My sense is that Iran is likely to demand a high price to get to a resolution, which is likely to remain politically untenable for the Trump administration.

Dr Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, Associate Fellow with Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, London

I do not think the latest strikes really alter Iranian calculations on the war. I think Tehran is preparing for an increased squeeze on its economy, and a continuation of the on and off attacks which we have seen over the past couple of months. Their intent will be to respond to these attacks in a proportionate manner in order not to spiral a larger conflict.

On the economic side, obviously this is likely to hurt the Iranian economy which has already been affected by the war and has had underlying structural issues anyway, as we know from the December and January demonstrations in Iran.

But I do not feel like there is the sense from the Iranian side that the economic squeeze is going to alter the Iranian calculation any time soon, including on any negotiations.

That does not mean Iran is not looking for an off ramp, but I think what we are seeing is that it is waiting for the US to go back to the MoU, or to at least offer some sort of concession. Tehran does not want to cave in to US pressure or alter its own approach in response to sanctions or additional attacks.

Nicholas Hopton, Distinguished Fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank in London and former UK ambassador to Iran

The latest spike in military action is not going to produce Iran's capitulation - it is just the latest twist. Economic pressure is also unlikely to work because China, Russia and many other countries which trade with Iran are not going to support unilateral US sanctions.

Iran can continue to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz - they have a thumb on the jugular of the global economy.

What is the White House's exit strategy?

Well, the US has already found it. If Trump was able to put a sustained effort into negotiating the deal outlined in June's MoU, that is the off-ramp.

Not only would a deal give the US a kind of victory because it would weaken the hardliners in the Islamic Republic, but also reassure everyone that Iran is not going to get a nuclear weapon.

There is a silver bullet in the MoU which is the lifting of all US sanctions on Iran.

What lifting those sanctions would do over time is weaken Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC). Economic engagement between the outside world and Iran in a new way would gradually force radical political and social change - so you end up with an Islamic regime, but of a very different nature.

Of course, that would not be straightforward to achieve, because of extensive IRGC penetration of the Iranian economy. But it should work, if given enough time and if the US and its partners exercised strategic patience which, sadly, is in short supply at this point.

For the time being, I think we're going to carry on with a messy, inconclusive situation that is bad for everyone.

GeneralTab.title: US jobs figures fuel rate rise bets as they beat expectations
GeneralTab.text:
A boost in hospitality and education employment drove the US economy to create tens of thousands more jobs than expected last month, latest figures suggest.

The number of roles added to the world's biggest economy increased by 162,000 in August, almost triple the 56,000 forecast by analysts.

The stronger jobs figures are likely to add to growing expectations that the Federal Reserve will increase interest rates later this month.

But President Donald Trump urged the Fed to cut rates saying the US should have the "LOWEST RATE of any country in the World".

"The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart - BE PATRIOTS for a change. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won't allow that to happen!", Trump said in a post on social media, external.

Last week, Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US central bank, signalled that rates could be hiked if policymakers were not confident price rises were easing for Americans.

Inflation, which measures price increases over time, remains above the Fed's 2% annual target, with prices up 3.4% in the past 12 months, according to the latest data.

The next interest rate decision will be made on 15-16 September. Rates were left unchanged between 3.5% and 3.75% in July for the fifth time in a row, but concerns over inflation remain due to the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which has caused as surge in global oil prices.

On Friday, US diesel prices hit an all-time high of $5.85 a gallon on average, compared to $3.71 a year ago.

But despite the cost of living rising, wages also appear to be increasing. In August, average hourly earnings for all employees were $37.75 on average, having increased 3.1%.

"Even the most committed dove would struggle to find anything in the August employment report to justify keeping interest rates unchanged," said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics.

He added that the strength in the jobs market meant that the latest inflation figures released next week would only need to be moderately above the Fed's target to fuel expectations of a September hike.

"A hike in rates just became a bit more likely," said Neil Birrell, chief investment office of investment firm Premier Miton.

Just over 60% of traders were betting on an interest rate hike in September, according to CME Group's "FedWatch" data.

An increase in employment during the final month of the summer in restaurants and bars, as well as in local government education ahead of the new school year, was behind August's labour market rebound.

Weaker job figures released earlier in the summer were revised up by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, revealing a stronger labour market than previously thought. Instead of the economy being deemed to have shed 23,000 jobs in July, some 44,000 were found to have been created in subsequent estimates.

While many more jobs were added, the US unemployment rate remained unchanged at 4.1% last month, with seven million out of work. Both measures have changed little over the year.

articles.title: Nigel Farage unveils small boats deal with Jordan Bardella at Reform conference
articles.text:
Nigel Farage has agreed a deal with France's hard-right National Rally (RN) party on returning migrants who attempt to cross the English Channel in small boats, should both parties win power.

It comes after Reform UK last month announced a plan to intercept boats and return migrants to French ports using the Royal Navy.

The proposed agreement with RN states that France would "ordinarily accept" those on board, and then repatriate them to their home country.

It was signed at Reform's annual conference in Birmingham by RN President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of presidential elections in April next year.

In a speech in the main conference hall, ahead of the deal being unveiled, Bardella told delegates that an RN government would "do everything in its power to ensure that France is no longer the gateway for illegal migration into the United Kingdom".

Hailing Farage as the UK's next prime minister, Bardella pledged to work with a potential future Reform government to tackle illegal migration.

The "memorandum of understanding" unveiled at the conference is a political document, but could be developed into a legal agreement between two future governments, if both parties win power.

It states: "The United Kingdom will intercept boats which have launched from French shores and entered British territorial waters and will return the persons on board to France.

"France will ordinarily accept these persons, who will be repatriated to their home country in accordance with the law in force in France concerning expulsion."

Under the proposals, illegal migrants who successfully arrive in the UK from France would be immediately detained and deported to their home country, rather than to France, under plans previously outlined by Reform.

Challenged during a news conference over whether the wording "ordinarily" meant some migrants would not be accepted by France, Farage said it was "legalese".

He argued the proposals would mean there was "no incentive" to pay a trafficker to cross the Channel, and "in very, very short order the business model is broken".

Farage said the "historic document" would "stop the boats forever".

Achieving this goal within the first 100 days of a Reform government is one of the party's key pledges.

Last month Emmanuel Macron's government hit out at Reform's proposals to use the Navy to return migrant boats to France, saying the they would violate the country's sovereignty and breach international law.

Opposition parties also branded the plan unworkable.

Labour has pointed to increased cooperation with France as contributing to the number of small boat crossings falling.

This includes extra officers being deployed to French beaches, and more funding to help prevent crossings.

Last year Sir Keir Starmer's government also signed a "one in, one out deal", which allows the UK to send some small boat-arrivals back to France, while agreeing to take the same number of people from France believed to have a legitimate claim to come to the UK.

articles.title: Falkland Islands: UK support 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims
articles.text:
The UK's position on the Falkland Islands is "unwavering", Downing Street has said after Argentina's president said the islands were "historically and legally" Argentinian.

Andy Burnham "fully supports the wishes of the islanders to remain a British overseas territory", a Downing Street spokesperson said.

Javier Milei said the "winds of change" favoured his country's claim to the islands and pledged sanctions on firms planning to exploit oil close to the islands.

A British and Israeli partnership due to begin exploration work on the Sea Lion oilfield said it didn't expect recent developments to affect its work in the region.

More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Britain and Argentina.

However in a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

When asked about if the prime minister believed the UK had the necessary forces to defend the sovereignty of the islands the spokesperson said "they will remain so far as long as the islanders wish".

"Our armed forces are on standby 24/7 to protect the UK and our interests", the spokesperson added.

Announcing his plan for sanctions in a national address on Thursday, Milei reiterated that the Falkland Islands were "historically and legally" Argentinian.

He said: "There can be no argument. They are part of the Argentine territory.

"The islanders on their usurped territory do not have a legitimate right to self-determination and any argument on any such self-determination is invalid."

Milei described the Sea Lion oilfield as a "clear and present danger", and said if Argentina does not act swiftly, "they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea – something that has never happened before."

He continued: "The Falklands are our future, we need to recover these islands which are nationally relevant. There is no other path forward".

It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.

A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government."

The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".

Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas.

"That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline".

On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.

Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review.

On Friday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the islands.

Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders."

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable".

"Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.

In an earlier statement, Downing Street said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands.

"We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources," it said.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "Britain does not surrender to bullies".

"If (Milei) wants a stronger Argentina, he should build its economy, not threaten others."

Although the US is formally neutral, Washington provided support for Britain's campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.

Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.

The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

articles.title: South Bank schools close early as hundreds attend A66 crash funeral
articles.text:
A number of schools have closed early amid safety concerns over a funeral linked to a crash which killed seven people.

The funeral of Jakub Matusiak, 23, one of five young men killed in the head-on collision with a marked police car on the A66, has been held near Middlesbrough.

The crash happened near South Bank on 22 August when a Volkswagen Passat travelled the wrong way on the dual carriageway and hit a police car. Two police officers, PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were also killed.

Head teachers had warned parents large crowds were expected to gather in the South Bank area for the funeral, with traffic disruption likely.

Cleveland Police said it was expecting the event to cause traffic disruption and delays, adding the force had plans in place to ensure public safety.

The decision to close the schools was taken following discussions between local head teachers and Redcar and Cleveland Council and was not a police recommendation, it said.

In an open letter, Conservative MP Laura Trott urged Education Secretary Lucy Powell to ensure local schools remained open and called for sufficient police support to be provided to keep schools in the area safe.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Ms Powell said she trusted head teachers to "make judgments that they need to make to keep their school community safe".

She said: "As Education Secretary, I want schools to be open. I want pupils attending schools all the time.

"These head teachers of these small number of schools have taken a very difficult decision, with the local authority and the police, for the safety of their school community to close early.

"What I would say, is that there are huge anxieties and worries in the communities."

She said she had been in touch with local MPs and Home Office ministers to put extra policing and resources in place to "calm those tensions down and to make those streets safe".

She added: "This is a very, very difficult and delicate situation, as you say, and I will always put the safety and wellbeing of children at the forefront of anything I do."

South Bank Primary School, St Peter's and Outwood Academy Normanby were among the schools which closed at lunchtime because of concerns about the impact of the funeral on pupils, staff and families.

Archway Academy in Teesville closed at 11:45 BST and St Margaret Clitherow's Catholic Primary School, in South Bank, at 12:15.

South Bank Primary School said it planned to close early "to ensure the safety and wellbeing of our pupils".

Head teacher Tammy Cooper said large numbers of people were expected in the area for the funeral at St John's Church on Normanby Road.

The school also said some pupils might feel "upset or anxious" about the funeral and that its pastoral team would be available to provide support.

Supt John Wrintmore from Cleveland Police said there was potential for traffic disruption and delays from 15:00 to 17:00 BST on Friday.

"This will affect areas of South Bank, Normanby Road through Teesville, Ormesby and Marton, and Acklam Road," he said.

"We are aware of some school closures in the area and have liaised with partners in the local authorities regarding the expected disruption today.

"Any decisions made by schools or other services to close has been a decision made by those organisations in isolation, and has not been a police recommendation.

"We are working closely with highways departments from the local authorities, who are leading on the traffic management for this event, in order to minimise disruption.

"There will be a proportionate visible police presence in the affected areas to ensure public safety, in line with our plans for any significant gathering."

A spokesperson for Redcar & Cleveland Borough Council said: "A number of schools in the South Bank area will close earlier than usual on Friday afternoon due to anticipated traffic congestion and transport disruption associated with a local funeral taking place in the area.

"The decision was made after careful consideration of the potential impact on home-to-school transport and the departure of pupils, staff and families at the end of the school day.

"Schools have worked with the Local Authority and transport providers to consider arrangements for pupils, including those who travel to and from specialist educational settings.

"We recognise that early closure may cause inconvenience for some parents and carers, and we thank them for their understanding and cooperation."

The decision comes after a vigil last week, for one of the young men who died, was followed by disorder in Haswell, County Durham, where a number of cars were set on fire.

The incident prompted criticism from MPs and police.

The Volkswagen Passat involved in the collision was being pursued by police until 10 seconds before the crash, according to the police watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said the Passat was believed to be using cloned registration plates.

Police said a total of 24 people had been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime, following the crash.
