articles.title: Private equity faces existential crisis in US as unsold companies pile up
articles.text:
Retail stalwarts Saks and Eddie Bauer filed for bankruptcy. Kmart and JoAnn Fabrics are gone for good, a trail of layoffs and disappointed customers in their wake. Hospital giant Steward Health Care collapsed, costing thousands of jobs and leaving several communities without a local hospital.

These once-trusted US companies have one thing in common: they were owned by private equity investors, who load companies with debt when they buy them and squeeze out profits as they restructure.

The business model is now facing an existential crisis that may have profound ramifications across the US.

Once fringe financial players, private equity investors have bought up vast swathes of US, UK, European and Australian industry, from local dentists to shopping mall anchors and fast-food chains and even the video games company EA.

In the US, these firms and the companies they own, employ more than 13 million people in everything from quirky startups like Dave’s Hot Chicken, Two Men and a Truck and School of Rock (all owned by Roark Capital) to the US’s largest pet retailer PetSmart (BC Partners) and classics Birkenstock (purchased by L Catterton in 2021) and Pyrex (owned by Centre Lane Partners).

Private equity investors also bought thousands of healthcare facilities in the US in recent years, including non-profit hospice care, rural hospitals and small-town dentists’ offices.

But this wave of buyouts is running smack into a wall of persistently high interest rates, rising buyout prices and pressure over moribund returns.

Private equity funds are sitting on a “record number of unsold companies, many of which they’ve been unable to sell … or at least unable to sell at the prices that they’re looking for”, said Jim Baker, the executive director of the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, an industry watchdog.

The US’s over 13,500 unsold companies in private equity portfolios include 2,563 consumer products and services companies, PitchBook data shows, and 1,536 healthcare companies. Hundreds of these have been sitting in PE portfolios for years longer than funds historically like to keep their investments.

A growing concern is that “eventually, the companies that have accumulated this much debt are going to collapse”, said Audrey Stienon, Industrial Policy Program Manager at Open Markets, an anti-monopoly thinktank that is examining private equity’s role in the greater economy.

And often, what private equity buys up “are really, really important businesses”, Stiennon said, providing jobs or vital services to local communities. “When they go down, either you need to bail them out, or you need to find someone to save them, or else you’re just stuck with fewer options for consumers down the line.”

Executives in the industry argue their deep pockets will help businesses weather any upcoming crisis. “Private equity-backed businesses face the same higher interest rates and economic pressures as other companies, but they also have committed investment partners that can provide additional capital and keep investing through difficult periods,” Will Dunham, the president and CEO of American Investment Council, an industry trade group, said in a statement.

“Ultimately, private equity only succeeds when the businesses it invests in succeed over the long term,” he said.

High rates, more competition

Think of private equity deals like buying a home, explains Brad Lipton, director of corporate power and financial regulation at the Roosevelt Institute. Investors buy the company with a hefty loan, like a mortgage, but plan to sell in a matter of years.

But unlike with a mortgage, the company is on the hook for making payments, not the buyer, and the buyer almost always plans to sell in a few years.

“Interest rates being unexpectedly high may have complicated exit strategies,” Lipton said.

Private equity firms promise investors higher returns than the stock market, in exchange for holding on to their money for a longer time period, generally 10 years, a business model that’s been the same for decades.

“What has changed is that the price of buying a target company has gone through the roof,” as the number of private equity funds increased, explains Rosemary Batt, a Cornell University management and labor professor who studies the industry’s impacts on workers and companies. Healthcare companies that once sold at 11 times EBITDA, a measure of enterprise value, are now priced at 18 times or more, for example.

That makes exiting the investment for a profit even more difficult on investors – and on customers and employees.

The higher prices for buyouts are “putting even more pressure on PE firms to squeeze the juice out of their portfolio companies”, Batt said, at a time when there’s almost no regulation governing how they do that.

“They can engage in financial engineering or just slash and burn on the operating side,” Batt said. “And it takes years for anyone to really see it.”

As they hold the company, these investors generally channel free cashflow to “creditors and equityholders, often constraining capital expenditures, worker training, and safety investments”, the University of Chicago’s Business Law Review warns. Tightening macroeconomic conditions can result in forced restructurings “that are costly and value‑destroying for the going concern”.

One vulnerable area is rural hospitals and other health provider chains which could face cashflow issues, making debt payments even more difficult, as the Trump administration’s cuts to the Affordable Care Act tax credits and Medicaid bite, warns Pablo Willis, spokesman for the Americans for Tax Fairness, which is advocating for changes to how private equity managers compensation and the firms overall are taxed.

“There’s bound to be a very negative effect,” he said.

A lack of financial transparency means it is hard to predict where or when, though. Companies owned by private equity generally don’t disclose their debt levels or other financials unless they go public or issue bonds themselves.

“By design, the industry takes place in the shadows,” Lipton said, so “everything has to begin with the thought that we don’t have a lot of clarity.”

More bankruptcies ahead

In a hint of the turmoil to come, private equity-backed companies have accounted for the lion’s share of big corporate bankruptcies in 2025 and the first half of 2026, research from the Private Equity Stakeholder Partnership shows.

The biggest determinant of whether or not a company will go bankrupt is leverage – the amount of borrowed money explains Edith Hotchkiss, a finance professor at Boston College. Private equity-backed companies are no more likely to default than other similarly leveraged firms, but their business models mean they have more debt.

They carry debt of about 50% of their enterprise value, recent studies show.

US consumers have felt private equity’s impact through the deteriorating quality of some fast-food outlets and disappearing stores as brands under PE ownership go broke.

Other industries have been hit too. More than 60% of big manufacturing bankruptcies in the US last year were private equity-backed, Baker said, as were an outsized number of healthcare bankruptcies.

Still, the number of PE-backed companies entering bankruptcy declined in 2025 from the year before, even as overall bankruptcies climbed, S&P found, as more companies pursued out-of-court settlements.

The entire process is disruptive by nature. “By definition there is not enough money to go around to pay” a company’s debts, Roosevelt’s Lipton said. “Someone is going to lose out and all too often that can be workers” who are owed pensions.

“It is a cause of concern for workers and consumers left holding the bag,” said Lipton.

Private equity operates without the rules and regulatory oversight of publicly traded companies. The industry has long argued that because it caters to sophisticated, high-net worth investors, it doesn’t need the same scrutiny.

But tens of thousands of layoffs, high bankruptcy rates, and the soaring wealth of dozens of private equity billionaires has created bipartisan momentum for more oversight, even before the current interest rate crisis. And Donald Trump’s push to allow everyday Americans to invest in the sector through their retirement plans has raised new concerns.

Congress’s June housing bill curbs private equity investments in single-family homes. November’s midterm elections, which are widely expected to deliver one or both houses of Congress to Democrats, could see a sea change for the industry in Washington, while several states are pursuing their own regulation.

“For private equity, the question increasingly is not whether Congress will investigate private equity firms and their practices, but rather where the scrutiny will turn to next,” corporate law firm Holland and Knight warned this month.

Multiple bills are circulating on Capitol Hill that would regulate how private equity is taxed, how it can invest in certain industries and how fund managers and investors can take profits. States’ bills would limit private equity in healthcare, scrutinize deals more closely and put caps on debt.

The “Let Kids Play” Act seeks to ban private equity from youth community sports, now a “$40bn industry dominated by private equity, with the singular goal of extracting as much profit as possible from families”, it contends.

The Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren, one of the industry’s most vocal critics in Washington, is leading a healthcare bill that seeks criminal penalties for “executives who loot health care entities like nursing homes and hospitals if that looting results in a patient’s death” and clawbacks of PE compensation.

Whether US consumers see some relief could depend on what state they live in, or what other issues Congress takes up in the fall. “Even Democrats will be very hard pressed to do much,” if they have any clout in Congress, Batt predicts, because they have so much on their plate. “The best opportunities right now are for local and state level initiatives,” she said.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Naomi Osaka and Jessica Pegula on influencers causing disruption in New York
articles.text:
Lights. Camera. Quiet please...

When it comes to etiquette in tennis, there are a fair few unwritten rules.

Apologising after winning a point from a net cord. Honesty around line calls, double bounces and double-hits. Post-match handshakes.

As for the spectators, it is common courtesy not to disturb the players during points.

Around 100 influencers and content creators have been granted accreditation for the tournament in New York - double the amount from last year.

Their presence has led to debate over how to balance bringing tennis to a new, different audience while respecting the game's etiquette.

"I definitely think it's cool to have a new demographic and I definitely think it helps grow the sport," world number four Coco Gauff said.

"But if you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans.

"I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport. That's all."

During two-time champion Naomi Osaka's first-round match on Arthur Ashe Stadium, one group held a photo shoot in their hospitality suite while play was going on.

The group turned on a portable ring light while Osaka was serving, leading to a reprimand from the umpire.

When Osaka returned on Thursday, the umpire had to remind the crowd several times to be quiet.

"Today the umpire told everyone to be quiet more than I've ever heard an umpire tell a crowd to be quiet," Osaka said.

"I tell people I normally just focus on the match and the court, but there was a moment where there was people shouting and you could hear it quite clearly.

"I think it bothered my opponent, too."

In one video, which has gone viral, a group can be seen speaking loudly as they film themselves during Osaka's first-round match on Tuesday, which led to the chair umpire calling for them to stop.

"I think obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport," Osaka said.

"I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette.

"It could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like my first-round match.

"Overall, I think there are huge positives. You want people to continue to grow the sport.

"I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette."

Arthur Ashe is the biggest tennis stadium in the world, and matches are often accompanied by a buzz of noise from conversations around the arena.

Some players love it. Some do not.

Men's seventh seed Daniil Medvedev, who has had a tricky relationship with the New York crowds in the past, believes whatever brings more eyes to tennis can only be a good thing.

"I think the more we try to raise awareness about tennis, the better it is, the more popular the sport is," the Russian said.

"The more the sport grows, the better it is. I trust USTA [tournament organisers the United States Tennis Association] with what they are doing.

"I think [there is] a lot more upside than downside, so go for it."

American 11th seed Frances Tiafoe praised the diversity of the crowd in New York.

"I think the Open is great because you get all types of people that want to come and watch tennis," he said.

"All different walks of life, different types of people, different type of occupations. Personally, I love that.

"I have no problem with anybody doing anything, coming to watch the tennis."

American world number three Jessica Pegula, however, said some of the behaviour had been "disrespectful".

"I can appreciate the influencers coming and showcasing the US Open experience," Pegula said.

"But I do think that it's tough when you see videos when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights.

"People are down there trying to perform. It's their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful.

"I think it's become a little too much this year.

"I can appreciate one side of it, but I think when you have the other side literally interrupting matches, it gets a little tough."

The US Open introduced a policy of free fan movement in 2024, meaning fans no longer have to wait to take their seats during changeovers.

A year later, the tournament was expanded to 15 days. The week before the singles draw is now marketed as a 'Fan Week', showcasing the revamped mixed doubles competition and exhibition matches between players past and present.

It is all part of what tournament chief executive Craig Tiley hopes will become "the tennis Disneyland".

Tiley, asked about influencers being accredited in a pre-tournament news conference, said: "We need to find ways of reaching new audiences, reaching people in a way that they connect with media today.

"The creation of the creator credential has been a key part of that because it's enabled us to talk to people in a way that they're listening. That's been a big focus."

Since the incident in Osaka's first match, there has been increased messaging on screens around the ground reminding people to "refrain from any activity that could disrupt the game, including noise levels, flash photography and ring lights".

The USTA said in a statement it "is always striving to grow tennis in this country and bring new audiences into the sport".

"We want all of our fans and guests to have an incredible time when they attend, but we also need to ensure they do not interfere with the action and competition on the court," it added.

"We are continually looking for ways to ensure fans in the stands know what is permitted and what is prohibited."

articles.title: Harry Kane: Europe's top scorer plays like a midfielder - we asked him to break down his game
articles.text:
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.

"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."

Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."

With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

articles.title: Italian Grand Prix: George Russell leads Charles Leclerc in Friday practice at Monza
articles.text:
Mercedes' George Russell topped Friday practice at the Italian Grand Prix from Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

Russell was 0.120 seconds quicker than Leclerc, with Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli, who will start the race from the back with a grid penalty, just 0.021secs behind the Ferrari.

McLaren's Lando Norris was fourth fastest from the second Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton and McLaren's Oscar Piastri.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen, still yet to win a race this year, was 0.818secs off the pace with ninth-fastest time, behind the Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad and Oliver Bearman's Haas.

Ferrari have introduced an upgraded engine for this race but its performance will not be clear until qualifying and the race.

But the Italian team have lagged behind Mercedes on engine performance all season - Hamilton says they have regularly been losing 0.4secs on the straights - so to be as close as they were on a track which is so power-sensitive because of the amount of time spent at full throttle was encouraging on the face of it.

articles.title: Jude Bellingham: England midfielder looks ready to show full potential at Real Madrid
articles.text:
Jude Bellingham has started the new season looking like a player with something to prove.

The 23-year-old's two goals and three assists have helped Real Madrid to an impressive start under new boss Jose Mourinho, with three wins from as many games.

Bellingham's performances, and the freedom he has been given in his new role, has attracted a lot of attention.

By playing higher up the pitch, he looks more free, more influential and closer to the role in which he first made such an impact at the Bernabeu in his debut 2023-24 season, where he scored 23 goals as his side won La Liga and the Champions League.

Bellingham's last two campaigns were less consistent, with his displays and attacking influence affected not only by a deeper role, but by recurring injuries. He had a long-standing shoulder problem that required surgery in 2025 and a hamstring issue that kept him out for 10 matches in 2026.

Now, however, he appears to be at peak fitness, ready to build on his impressive World Cup form for England and showcase the full extent of his talent.

Since returning this summer to take charge of the club for a second spell, Mourinho has made an important adjustment in reducing the defensive workload that previously meant Bellingham had to cover huge areas of the pitch.

"We've organised the team differently," he said after Real Madrid's 4-0 La Liga win over Malaga.

"Bellingham sometimes defended like a second left-back last season. I told him I do not want to see that anymore. I made a deal with him."

The Portuguese manager has used Bellingham primarily as a number 10 in a 4-2-3-1 system, operating behind French striker Kylian Mbappe and with the freedom to move across the attacking line.

That gives the England midfielder a clearer role. Rather than constantly moving between midfield, defence and attack, he can spend more time in the areas where he is most dangerous.

"For me, this is his position, with his connection with the forwards, he can score goals," added Mourinho.

"He has to play close to the goal. Playing at number six or number eight, we're losing his closeness to the goal. I like this Jude."

It has meant Bellingham can receive the ball between the lines, carry it forward, combine with the forwards and make late runs into the penalty area.

Just as importantly, he is being given greater freedom to decide when to move.

Bellingham has explained the difference himself in an interview with Real Madrid TV.

"I feel more free to decide when to drop back, when to stay up or when to get into the box," he said. "I think this is the best position for me."

Mourinho still expects him to press and recover possession, but the difference is where that work begins.

Instead of dropping deep towards his own penalty area, Bellingham can now use his energy to press opponents higher up the pitch.

When Madrid win the ball, he is already closer to the forwards. That allows him to connect midfield with attack and provide another player who can combine with Mbappe and Vinicius Jr.

It also explains why Mourinho has been keen to stress Madrid's attacking players must work together rather than operate as individuals.

"The team dynamic is about 11, not 2+9," he said.

The midfielder also described working with Mourinho as a "dream", having previously only met the former Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham manager once before his appointment.

There is clearly an early understanding and respect between the two.

Mourinho has repeatedly spoken about Bellingham's importance to his plans, describing him as a "unique and super important player" with qualities that include physical, mental and tactical.

He also suggested Bellingham should be one of the players in the running for the Ballon d'Or.

"He is a unique kind of player and extremely important for the team," said Mourinho.

"His mental strength, tactical ability, the way he recovers the ball, the way he pressures, the way he plays up front, I am very happy."

For Mourinho, that versatility is part of what makes Bellingham so valuable. He can press, recover possession, score, contribute in the air and drive the team forward.

The Real boss has also pointed to Thomas Tuchel's use of Bellingham at the World Cup as an example of how to get the best out of him.

Bellingham was one of England's standout players, finishing with seven goals and an assist in his eight appearances, and his attacking qualities were allowed to flourish.

That experience also appears to have given the player a confidence boost, particularly as he rejoined Madrid later than most of his team-mates and had less time to prepare for the new campaign.

Although Real's three league wins - scoring 10 goals and conceding two - are only a small sample, and the demands will increase as the season progresses amid Champions League football, the early signs are very positive.

For Bellingham, whose huge strength has always been his ability to affect almost every part of a game, Mourinho's system has given him more control over where that influence is used.

After a difficult couple of seasons following the high standards he set in his first year, the England midfielder is enjoying his football again.

"I'm having a lot of fun, I'm really enjoying my football, and that's why I'm performing well," he told club media.

If he continues in this vein with Mourinho's continued support, it could turn out to be his best season yet.

articles.title: Rangers-Celtic: No away fans for SPFL Old Firm matches this season
articles.text:
There will be no away supporters for Celtic and Rangers derbies in the Scottish Premiership or Premier Sports Cup this season.

The "temporary arrangement" was reached following talks between the Glasgow clubs and the Scottish Professional Football League (SPFL).

It follows the Scottish FA's independent review into events surrounding last term's Scottish Cup quarter-final at Ibrox, which was marred by unrest and pitch incursions from both sets of fans.

Rangers host Celtic in the Premier Sports Cup on 13 September, with the city rivals meeting at Celtic Park in the league a week later.

Rangers had proposed a reduced away allocation of 300 for the impending cup tie, with Celtic rejecting the offer.

The crowd disorder on 8 March came after a penalty shootout win for Celtic, when around 8,000 visiting supporters had been present.

That figure was much larger than recent Old Firm league derbies, with ticketing rules different for the Scottish Cup.

The Scottish FA announced last month that both clubs would have to play their next Scottish Cup home games behind closed doors.

Announcing the measures, a statement from the SPFL said: "This temporary arrangement will allow both clubs, together with the SPFL, Police Scotland and other relevant stakeholders, to give proper consideration to the findings and recommendations of the independent review, take forward the necessary actions and ensure sufficient time is available to plan future fixtures thoroughly.

"It will also provide greater certainty for supporters and those involved in matchday planning, while avoiding repeated uncertainty around ticketing arrangements for individual fixtures.

"All parties have committed to working constructively during this period, with safety and security remaining the priority."

articles.title: England cricket squads: Aneurin Donald and Henry Crocombe called up for Sri Lanka series
articles.text:
England have named the uncapped Aneurin Donald and Henry Crocombe in their squads for the white-ball series against Sri Lanka.

Derbyshire opener Donald has been included in the 16-player squad for the three-match T20 series, while Sussex seamer Crocombe makes the 16-man line-up for the three one-day internationals.

Donald scored 489 runs in 12 matches captaining Derbyshire Falcons in the Vitality Blast and hit the most sixes in this year's competition with 37.

He also helped Trent Rockets to the final of the Hundred, which the 29-year-old's side lost to Manchester Super Giants.

Crocombe, 24, has taken hat-tricks in his past two County Championship matches and has three five-wicket hauls this season.

England men's national selector Marcus North said the pair are "two promising players who have earned their places on the back of impressive performances in domestic cricket".

He added: "Aneurin has had an exceptional season for Derbyshire in the Vitality Blast and also with Trent Rockets in The Hundred while Henry is a player we have had an eye on all summer."

Meanwhile England all-rounder Jacob Bethell will again be absent after he "underwent successful surgery on his injured knee earlier this week".

He is targeting the white-ball series against Australia in November for his comeback.

Bethell sustained his injury in the ODI series against India in the summer and missed the Test series against Pakistan.

He is also expected to be absent for an ODI tri-series against hosts Pakistan and Sri Lanka in Lahore and Rawalpindi in October.

Batter Phil Salt is unavailable because of a right quad injury, while bowler Jamie Overton is in both squads after missing the white-ball series against India earlier with a thigh injury.

articles.title: Katie Taylor vs Flora Pili: Tears and tricolours - an inside look at Irish icon's final fight week
articles.text:
Katie Taylor smiles as she sits down for her fight-week media commitments, but her eyes give her away.

On Saturday, she faces unbeaten Frenchwoman Flora Pili at Croke Park, bringing down the curtain on a career that has gone from disguising herself as a boy in a sport that barred women, to Olympic gold and undisputed titles.

The weight of a lifetime in the ring is catching up with an Irish icon preparing to step away.

"I thought I was handling all the emotions until today," the 40-year-old tells BBC Sport.

Taylor's usual defensive armour is slipping as the reality of a Croke Park farewell sets in. There is no next opponent waiting in the shadows, only 80,000 roaring voices, a sea of green, white and orange tricolours and the final chapter of a transcendent career.

"This is the stuff of dreams and I'm pinching myself that it's happening," Taylor adds.

"I look back at my career and think how remarkable it has been. The highs, the lows, the failures, the disappointments and the successes."

Taylor has never hidden her disdain for the circus of fight-week theatre, preferring the sanctuary of the gym.

But this week she has welled up under the glare of the cameras and stayed a fraction longer during face-offs to absorb the magnitude of the moment.

"Every fighter in the world wishes they were in this position," she says.

"I'm just blown away from the support from this country. I don't think there are many other countries where 80,000 show up for a female athlete.

"The crowd - hearing 'ole ole ole' one last time - feeling the atmosphere, seeing the tricolours all over the place..."

The emotion has rippled through her inner circle. Eddie Hearn choked up mid-sentence during the final news conference when it dawned on him this was the last time he would experience a Taylor fight week.

"When it's all said and done you will look at your belts, you might look at your bank balance. But you will sit there, close your eyes and recall all those incredible moments in your life that made you cry," he later told BBC Sport.

"I will cry on the ring walk. I will cry in the [post-fight] interview."

Taylor is softly spoken and laser-focused, but this week has unlocked a relaxed side of her rarely seen by the public. She joked during final media commitments about flipping the table just to disrupt the monotony.

"Katie Taylor is one of the funniest people I've met. Unexpectedly funny. She's so strong and determined. But people who know, she's very jovial, she's got great energy and I think she's soaking all that up," Hearn adds.

All week, her nearest and dearest have insisted she is Ireland's greatest ever sportsperson. Manager Brian Peters jokingly issued an apology to Roy Keane, reassuring him he was a close second.

From taxi drivers gridlocked in traffic to those pulling pints in Temple Bar, everyone across the capital is frantically seeking spare tickets.

But even with Taylor's popularity, selling out Croke Park is no easy feat. While she has a reputation for being fiercely zoned into her training rather than chasing the spotlight, she has put work into the promotion. And perhaps even enjoyed it.

Peters spearheaded an exhausting, 1,500-mile island-wide bus tour spanning all 32 counties, completing dozens of radio chats and community stops to promote the swansong.

"No-one works as hard as Katie," Peters says. "Those four days she did not stop working. These stadiums don't sell out on their own."

When thousands mobbed the gates at a Kilkenny stop on an unforgiving timetable, Taylor refused to turn a blind eye. "Ah Brian, we can't drive past them," Peters recalls Taylor insisting, pulling the vehicle over to take group photos.

That effort has helped turn Saturday into something bigger than a boxing event. About 80% of those inside Croke Park will be attending a live fight for the first time, while 65% of tickets were sold outside Dublin.

With the bout also being shown on free-to-air TV across Ireland, Taylor's farewell - which will include music from one of the nation's biggest pop groups, Westlife - has become a national celebration.

Pili has spent the week quietly slipping through corridors while the media storm swirls around Taylor.

The undefeated challenger arrives with a 12-0 record and a hunger to create her own story.

"I have nothing to lose and everything to win," Pili, 29, said.

But with fight-week media commitments cleverly packed into the start of the week, Taylor has been given the space to get the tears and emotion out of her system.

"I don't think I can prepare for what happens on Saturday, but I'm going to try and keep emotions in check and try and enjoy the ringwalk. But the most important thing is to win," she says.

Asked how she will feel when the dust settles on Sunday morning, Taylor says: "Probably a bit relieved - I don't have to take any more punches again."

The tears may come again at the end of Saturday night. This time, though, the final bell really will mean the end.

articles.title: Richarlison: Striker's omission not my decision says Spurs boss Roberto de Zerbi
articles.text:
Tottenham Hotspur manager Roberto de Zerbi says it was not his decision to leave Richarlison out of the club's Premier League squad.

While injured duo Xavi Simons and Wilson Odobert were included in the 25-man list that Spurs submitted to the Premier League on Thursday, the Brazil forward was a notable omission after a turbulent week.

On Saturday, De Zerbi said the 29-year-old had asked to leave Tottenham and he was close to joining former club Everton before Tuesday's transfer deadline but a deal fell through.

"It was not my decision. It is the normal decision," said the Italian boss.

"I think Richarlison, he decided everything alone. He spoke with me at the beginning of the pre-season and told me his idea and desire was to leave.

"At the end we go to bring another striker [in] and like I said at the beginning of the pre-season, I want to keep the players, just the players that want to stay and be proud and with the right passion to stay here.

"Then for everything and other problems, it is not my business and not my job. It is the responsibility of the club.

"I can't say nothing because I didn't decide anything. The message of Richarlison from the beginning of the season has been very clear. I accepted that and for me [there is[ nothing [to say]."

Trabzonspor have been linked with a move for Richarlison with the transfer deadline for Turkish clubs set to close at 22:00 BST on Friday.

Clubs in Saudi Arabia can sign players until Sunday, but if the ex-Everton forward remains at Spurs, he will be ineligible to play in the Premier League.

articles.title: Pierre Gasly loses Monaco podium after McLaren and Red Bull win appeals
articles.text:
McLaren and Red Bull have won their appeals against the result of the Monaco Grand Prix after a controversy over multiple incorrect pit-lane speeding penalties.

The victory means Alpine's Pierre Gasly loses the podium he was awarded after an appeal by his French team that overturned two five-second penalties.

Gasly, who finished third on the road, is dropped back to the seventh place he received in the official results.

Alpine, unlike the other teams involved, did not serve the penalties in the race because they believed they had been applied incorrectly.

Red Bull's Isack Hadjar is returned to third place and McLaren's Oscar Piastri fourth, with Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad moving up to fifth and sixth.

Alpine said they felt they had been "unjustly punished" by the decision.

Alpine executive director Flavio Briatore used a news conference at the Italian Grand Prix on Friday to say one of the four court of appeal judges was "linked to the McLaren company".

Briatore pointed to his presence at a charity event in California in 2018 for a group that Briatore alleged had received "two or three McLaren cars".

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella described Briatore's remarks as "insulting".

He added: "If anybody makes these kind of allegations, which seem quite serious, they are going to have to take the responsibility for what they are saying in a public forum. The hearing, the whole international court of appeal was conducted to the highest standards, and we should not question this case like has been done."

The FIA says its international court of appeal, which heard the case, is "an independent body with its own administration detached from the main structure of the FIA".

Judges in each case are selected from a pool of 36 which are elected by the FIA general assembly after a nomination process.

The verdict does not fully address the multiple effects of a series of pit-lane speeding penalties.

These affected the results of many drivers in the race, including Mercedes' George Russell.

The Briton was dropped out of the points for a penalty he received for not correctly serving a pit-lane speeding penalty.

The court of appeal decision, external rests on its conclusion that the parameters for measuring a limit could not be changed in the midst of a grand prix weekend once competitors had been informed of them.

The discrepancy between the official F1 measurement and the possible shorter distance did not mean that the official measurement was incorrect, the court said.

While it was concluded after the race that a shorter line was possible, the court of appeal ruled that "sporting fairness absolutely precludes the retrospective replacement" of an established calibration parameter "by a different geometric or measurement approach for the purpose of re-adjudicating an individual competitor's result".

The controversy arose from the fact that there was a 77-centimetre discrepancy between the officially measured distance of the pit lane and the real shortest route a driver could take.

It was established at Alpine's appeal in June that Gasly had not exceeded the pit-lane speeding limit by this new measurement, which was why the penalty was overturned.

However, McLaren appealed on the grounds of sporting fairness and their own competitive interests, as Piastri had lost two points as a consequence of the situation.

The Australian was one of several drivers who did serve a five-second pit-lane speeding penalty.

The court of appeal verdict rests on the following conclusions:

F1 is designated by the FIA to measure the pit-lane speed limit, which is applied by "average speed over the relevant timing sector rather than instantaneous speed".

The distance applied should be the same for each car.

Although it was later established that Gasly never exceeded the 60km/h limit over a shorter distance it was possible to take, the "benchmark cannot be retrospectively displaced for one competitor after the competition has been conducted against it".

Although F1 concluded after the event that a shorter distance, measured by a different method, meant it should have selected a different line for its calculation, that did not mean the original calculation was inaccurate of itself.

The pit-lane length applied "was physically tape-measured, checked before being entered, used throughout free practice sessions and the race, specifically re-examined when concerns were raised before the race, and reconfirmed again during the race when the stewards sought reassurance. At no point did F1 advise the competitors, race control or the stewards that a different distance parameter should apply".

"The enforcement regime… is workable only if the benchmark against which all competitors calibrate is common, stable and applied equally throughout the competition".

"Once the official timekeeper has established and adopted the distance parameter used… and competitors have been required to calibrate their cars and conduct the competition by reference to that common parameter, sporting fairness and equal treatment require that the parameter remains fixed".

Alpine said in a statement: "While we disagree with the decision, and still fully maintain that car 10 (Gasly) did not exceed the pit-lane speed limit at any point during the race, the team acknowledges the decision of the judging panel from the recent hearing in Paris.

"While the result is not what we had hoped for, as we feel that we have been unjustly punished, the team is firmly focused on continuing to improve its performance on track and remains in a close and very competitive championship fight."

McLaren said: "We welcome the decision of the FIA international court of appeal, a decision which provides important clarity for teams and all the sport's stakeholders and helps protect the integrity of the sport and trust in its regulatory framework.

"Our appeal was not directed at any competitor or at the FIA. It was brought, and pursued to its conclusion, in the interests of the sport and to support the consistent and fair application of the regulations for all participants."

The court of appeal did not address the question of whether the pit-lane speeding penalties awarded to Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, Russell and Piastri were correct under the established measurement, or whether their cars ever physically exceeded the 60km/h limit.

That was not relevant to the bounds of the hearing, which was to address McLaren's and Red Bull's protest against the decision to rescind Gasly's penalty.

Mercedes also contend that Russell never exceeded 60km/h. He was running ahead of Hadjar and Gasly before his first penalty.

He was demoted out of the points because Mercedes failed to correctly serve the penalty at a subsequent pit stop. That offence earned a drive-through penalty which dropped him to 12th place.

Alpine say they have sent the trophy for third place over to Red Bull's Milton Keynes base, and that they are considering their options as to whether to take the case further.

Their only remaining likely course of action, should they wish to pursue it, would be to go to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

articles.title: Premier League predictions: Chris Sutton v Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno - & AI
articles.text:
Arsenal and Chelsea have both made 100% winning starts to the new season - but something has to give when they meet at Emirates Stadium on Sunday.

"I suspect Chelsea will give Arsenal lots of the ball and try to counter-attack quickly," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"The Blues have got some brilliant creativity in Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro, but the fact they are vulnerable at the back could undermine them."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week three, he takes on Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno, who is a Leicester City fan.

Kasabian's ninth album, Act III, is out on Friday, 4 September, and they tour the UK in December.

Do you agree with their scores? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions.

It has been an eventful decade for Foxes fans since they won the Premier League title in 2016 - and not always an enjoyable one.

Since then, they have seen their side reach the Champions League quarter-finals, lift the FA Cup and Community Shield, win promotion from the Championship and suffer three relegations, including last season when they went down to League One.

What comes next?

"Promotion!" said Serge. "It has to be. I love the play-offs, so a win at Wembley would do me."

A new-look Leicester side took their first step towards bouncing back when they picked up their opening win of the season against Plymouth on Tuesday, but Serge added Russell Martin's youthful side will need time to fully find their feet in the third tier.

"I hope they get it," he said. "Patience is so important in football, and young teams should play with no fear."

Chris Sutton and Serge Pizzorno were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Portman Road, 20:00 BST

My daughter's old maths teacher, Mr Fields, is an Ipswich fan and he is very excited about how ambitious the club has been since getting promoted. I think all their supporters must be the same.

Ipswich have spent almost £200m on a stack of new signings to try to stay in the Premier League and, watching them, it is clear they are not just planning to park the bus.

They will be confident for this game after beating Sunderland at home on the opening weekend and I am expecting them to have a real go at Liverpool too.

It will be interesting to see if new signing Bradley Barcola starts for the Reds, who seem to have a lot of attacking players who like to play off the left.

Boss Andoni Iraola has plenty of attacking options, but I still have concerns about them defensively, while his players adjust to his front-foot pressing style.

I am sure he will get it right eventually, but at the moment they are leaking goals and creaking at the back.

My gut feeling is Ipswich will score, but Liverpool will still edge the win after two successive 2-2 draws. If their attack clicks, it will be hard to keep them out.

Sutton's prediction: 1-2

Serge's prediction: 1-2

AI's prediction: 1-3

St James' Park, 12:30

Newcastle have started the season superbly with four points, and it feels like they have changed the mood at St James' Park after a difficult summer.

There's no doom and gloom about the place despite them losing several key players and, after predicting they would lose their first two games, I feel differently about their prospects now.

Things can change very quickly of course and a home defeat by Bournemouth would see a lot of that optimism disappear. But, so far, I've been really impressed by Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa looks like he has got his confidence back.

I like the way new manager Matthias Jaissle has set them up to hit teams on the counter-attack, and Nico Gonzalez looks like a sensible signing too.

I called Newcastle 'a development club' before their first game, because of the type of players they have bought and sold this summer, but while their midfield is quite youthful, they have now got Nico in there to give them a bit of extra clout.

This is still a tricky game to call, however.

Bournemouth haven't won yet, but only because they have let leads slip away late on, first against Manchester City and then at home to Everton.

Cherries boss Marco Rose is another manager who likes to play on the front foot and they are certainly capable of getting something here, even though I have gone for a home win.

Sutton's prediction: 2-1

Serge's prediction: 2-0

AI's prediction: 2-1

Gtech Community Stadium, 15:00

I was spot on with my predictions for both of these teams last week, but I still don't feel very confident about calling the outcome of this game.

Brentford are a brilliant counter-attacking side who seem especially strong at home.

I was erring towards backing the Bees to win, like they did in this fixture last season, but then had second thoughts.

I backed the Black Cats to win their first two matches (see the table based on Sutton's predictions at the bottom of the page) because they are a well-organised team, with plenty of physicality and also a threat up top.

My concern for them is what happens when European football starts, but that hasn't happened yet. I don't see them losing this.

Sutton's prediction: 1-1

Serge's prediction: 1-0

AI's prediction: 1-1

Amex Stadium, 15:00

I am not really sure what to make of Brighton yet. They smashed Aston Villa on the opening weekend but then lost to Chelsea despite dominating possession in what was a really strange game.

Leeds can be quite cagey on the road under Daniel Farke, but they are very good at what they do, and they will be a threat on the break.

I am still going with Brighton to win because they are playing with freedom at the moment, but I don't see them keeping a clean sheet and this is going to be close.

Sutton's prediction: 2-1

Serge's prediction: 2-1

AI's prediction: 2-0

Craven Cottage, 15:00

Neither of these teams have got a point so far, as I predicted.

On top of his side's poor start to the season, one of the problems for Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage will be dealing with Ismaila Sarr after he did not get a move to Liverpool before the transfer window shut.

My worry for Fulham is they have become a Real Madrid feeder team, and their boss Alvaro Arbeloa has already got issues with his squad.

He stuck the boot into his players after their defeat by Sunderland, questioning their mentality.

A first win would be massive for both new managers, but I don't think either of them will get it here.

Sutton's prediction: 1-1

Serge's prediction: 2-0

AI's prediction: 1-1

Etihad Stadium, 15:00

This is a tale of two Citys - one of whom has made the best of starts to the season, while the other has had the worst.

Manchester City wiped the floor with Crystal Palace last week but it was their comeback to beat Bournemouth at the Etihad which felt bigger, because it was the beginning of a new era under Enzo Maresca.

In contrast, Coventry City have had a terrible time. Not their 3-0 opening defeat at Arsenal, because they can forget about that, but they must feel so deflated after losing 1-0 at home to another promoted side in Hull last time out.

That must have hurt.

This game is more like the Arsenal one, in that no-one is expecting Coventry to get anything, but the upshot is they are likely to be left without a point or even a goal after their first three games.

There were some doubts about Manchester City after the way they lost the Community Shield against Arsenal, but they look a different proposition already.

Maresca has made more signings in the past few days, including Enzo Fernandez from his old club Chelsea for £125m. I've heard people question whether Fernandez is worth the big money that City paid, but Maresca knows him well and I see him as a great addition to their midfield.

I said before the Bournemouth game I didn't think they could win the title without Rodri, but they have rebuilt their midfield now with Fernandez and Ayyoub Bouaddi joining Elliot Anderson as new signings, and they have got real strength in there now.

I like Erling Haaland's new haircut too. It suits him far more than a ponytail. He looks a bit rougher and tougher and I don't think Coventry will keep him out.

Sutton's prediction: 3-0

Serge's prediction: 4-0

AI's prediction: 4-0

City Ground, 15:00

Nottingham Forest are waiting for their first win under Oliver Glasner but I felt they were unlucky to lose against Leeds and also to only draw at Liverpool.

I have been very disappointed with Roberto de Zerbi's Tottenham so far, however, and not just because of their poor results.

When he came in at Brighton, De Zerbi built an amazing team in a short space of time and they were great to watch even if they made a few mistakes along the way.

In contrast, we still don't know what his Spurs team are about, even though they have spent an absolute fortune on players.

I think that's on De Zerbi because, although new players take time to gel, his side have put in two really insipid performances so far.

He has put that down to the team not being fully fit and blamed their pre-season schedule, but they should still be doing much better than they are - with no points and no goals so far.

Other clubs, with new managers as well as lots of new players, look much more organised so it is not an excuse.

Still, Spurs have surely got to improve soon, which is why I have got them down to pick up a first point here.

Sutton's prediction: 1-1

Serge's prediction: 1-3

AI's prediction: 1-2

MKM Stadium, 17:30

Hull will be on such a high after winning their first two games, and that makes this game even harder to predict.

The Tigers are really well organised and are not bothered about how much possession they have, they are just bothered about being effective when they do get the ball.

They defend the box brilliantly but there will still be a few weeks this season where teams run all over them because of the way they are set up.

Aston Villa won't necessarily do that, but I still think they will come out on top despite their poor start to the new campaign.

Ollie Watkins is a big loss but they have got Nicolas Jackson in to lead their line, who I think is a good signing.

It took Villa six games to register their first league win last season, but they won't have to wait as long this time.

Sutton's prediction: 0-2

Serge's prediction: 1-0

AI's prediction: 1-2

Emirates Stadium, 16:30

Arsenal were a bit clunky last time out against Aston Villa, while I love what Xabi Alonso is doing at Chelsea.

He doesn't care about possession, and that's not how Chelsea try to get results.

It's strange because I had a look at how his Bayer Leverkusen side lined up when they won the Bundesliga, and they were pretty dominant possession-wise.

So, it is quite alarming when you look at the two league games Chelsea have played and see how much of the ball they haven't had. Against Fulham they only had 38% possession and then against Brighton it was down to 25%.

I don't know whether that is by design or by just not having the players to dominate. They are still free-scoring, but they are conceding loads of goals too.

Whatever the reason, I don't see it changing here. Arsenal are so powerful and the only question mark around them is if they are a forward or two short.

Even so, you would not exactly say they have a real weakness anywhere. The beauty of Mikel Arteta's side is they can play in different ways.

They demolished Manchester City in the Community Shield with some pure football, and played some nice stuff against Coventry too, but then they were able to grind out a win at Aston Villa as well.

Ultimately, whether they are free-flowing or not, their organisation should see them through this game too.

Sutton's prediction: 3-1

Serge's prediction: 2-1

AI's prediction: 2-2

Chris picked up his first win of the season after getting seven correct results - including three exact scores - from the 10 matches in week two.

After a slow start, five of his correct results - and two of his exact scores - came in the five games on Sunday and Monday.

That gave him a total of 160 points, enough to hold off a strong challenge from the BBC readers and AI.

The collective efforts of the readers helped them get six correct results, with two exact scores, for 120 points.

Like Chris, AI managed seven correct results, but with only one exact score, leaving it on 100 points.

Chris' guest, Royal Blood drummer Ben Thatcher, did not fare so well. He got four correct results with no exact scores, and ended up with 40 points.

"It's not how you start the weekend, it's how you finish it," Sutton said. "I am burying AI at the moment, which is a lovely feeling."

Everyone was right about three of the fixtures - Manchester City's win at Crystal Palace, Manchester United's victory over Ipswich and Arsenal's success at Aston Villa.

There were only two fixtures where none of our predictors picked the right outcome - Liverpool's draw with Nottingham Forest and Hull's win at Coventry.

From almost 37,000 predictions for the latter, only around 5,000 (15%) of you backed the Tigers to take the three points, and fewer than 1,500 (4%) went for them to win by a 1-0 scoreline.

articles.title: FA Cup: From playing with Marcus Rashford at Man Utd to non-league & new career
articles.text:
A Tuesday night in Workington in late August and Joe Riley leads his Warrington Rylands team-mates out for a match at the Fibrus Community Stadium in the seventh tier of English football.

Rylands race into a 2-0 lead in Cumbria before losing 3-2 after having two players sent off in a chaotic Northern Premier League Premier Division encounter played in front of 638 supporters.

"A few years back I wouldn't speak for 24 hours if I lost," says Riley, whose side host Hyde United in the first qualifying round of the FA Cup on Saturday (15:00 BST).

"Now if we lose, it's not ideal, but there's always another game around the corner."

It is 10 years since Riley, then aged 19, started at left-back for injury-hit Manchester United against Danish side Midtjylland in the Europa League at Old Trafford, the same match Marcus Rashford also made his first start for the club.

While Rashford has gone on to rack up more than 400 club appearances and earn 78 England caps since scoring two in that emphatic 5-1 win, external a decade ago, Riley left United at 21 with two first-team appearances to his name - and drifted down the leagues after bad luck with injuries.

While recovering from one injury too many at League Two Walsall, he started studying for a new career.

Now aged 29, he sells life insurance, income protection, critical illness and injury cover as a financial protection advisor - while playing non-league football.

"I lived with Scott McTominay for six years, and Marcus and I also came through the academy together," Riley tells BBC Sport.

"These people were like family to me.

"Of course I would have liked to have played more games for United but things didn't work out like that.

"I don't dwell on the past - I'm just happy that it happened. I've now got my foot in the door for the next chapter of my life. I'm progressing with another career that's setting me up for the rest of my life."

Riley grew up in Lytham, Lancashire, and joined United at the age of six.

He went on to play for the under-18s with Rashford, Scotland midfielder McTominay, now at Napoli, and England goalkeeper Dean Henderson, who is at Crystal Palace.

It was while Riley was playing regularly for the under-21s, aged 19, that he - and 18-year-old Rashford - got their big break in February 2016 under Louis van Gaal.

Having come on as a substitute in a 3-0 win at Shrewsbury Town in the fifth round of the FA Cup three days earlier, Riley was named in the starting line-up for a Europa League last-32 tie with Midtjylland, along with Rashford.

United had lost the first leg in Denmark 2-1 and, missing several key players through injury, were in danger of going out of Europe.

England forward Wayne Rooney was among those out receiving treatment along with goalkeeper David de Gea, winger Antonio Valencia and defender Chris Smalling.

"The day before the game Van Gaal stuck the starting XI on a board at a team meeting," recalls Riley.

The young player carefully went down the list of familiar names.

Michael Carrick, Daley Blind, Juan Mata, Jesse Lingard, Memphis Depay... Joe Riley!

"I remember thinking: 'Oh my God'. It was a dream come true."

Riley's mum, Derren, and sister, Sophie, were in the 58,609 crowd at Old Trafford to watch him play 79 minutes.

By the time United's No 49 received a standing ovation when he was replaced by Argentina left-back Marcos Rojo, who was returning after three months out with a dislocated shoulder, Van Gaal's side were leading 3-1 on the night (4-3 agg), before scoring a further two late goals to book a last-16 European tie with Liverpool.

"I had a really good game but I do remember thinking that could be my last for the first team, because the likes of Rojo and Luke Shaw were working their way back from injuries," he says.

Riley's hunch proved correct.

While Rashford went on to play several more times that season, including United's FA Cup final win over Crystal Palace at Wembley, Riley did not appear again for the senior side.

He continued to train with the first team even after Van Gaal was sacked and replaced by Jose Mourinho in May 2016, and was named captain of the under-23s.

By 2017, however, injuries were already starting to disrupt his career.

A damaged hamstring delayed a loan move to Sheffield United and, when the player did eventually arrive at Bramall Lane, the loan was cut short after he dislocated his shoulder.

Riley's 15 years at United ended on 25 May 2018, two years after that magical night against Midtjylland.

While former under-18s team-mate Rashford was preparing to go to the World Cup in Russia with England, Riley joined League One Bradford City on a two-year contract.

Riley's mum can be seen at Warrington Rylands matches supporting her son, just as she did on that cold February Thursday night at Old Trafford all those years ago.

"I will forever be grateful to Manchester United," says Riley, who is engaged to be married to Elizabeth, his partner for the past seven years, next summer in the south of France.

"United turned me into the person I am today - I've got them to thank for that."

And what about Rashford. Is he still in touch with his former academy team-mate?

"I don't have Marcus' number so we don't message. If I bumped into him, I've no doubt it would be just the same as all those years ago when we were growing up together.

"I saw [United boss] Michael Carrick in Portugal this summer and we had a really good chat."

Although he has moved on with his life, Riley does have one regret from his time with United.

Having played a small part in their triumphant 2016 FA Cup campaign, the young United substitute at Shrewsbury wishes he had pressed the club for a winners' medal.

"Had I done so then I probably would have received one," he says.

"I didn't go to Wembley because I wasn't in the squad for the final. At the time I was young and naive, thinking I'd have plenty more opportunities to get a medal.

"In the end I only got to play two first-team games for Manchester United. No-one though will ever be able to take those memories away from me."

articles.title: Jonny Brownlee retires from triathlon at 36
articles.text:
Former world and Olympic champion Jonny Brownlee has retired at the age of 36.

The Briton won Olympic bronze at London 2012, silver at Rio 2016 and gold in the mixed relay at Tokyo 2020.

He is also a six‑time world champion and won mixed team relay gold at the 2014 Commonwealth Games.

Brother Alistair, a double Olympic champion, retired at the age of 36 in 2024.

"I've been thinking about it for a while. I've won more than I ever thought I'd ever achieve," Jonny told BBC Sport.

"One thing I'm really proud of is we full on committed to winning Olympic medals and delivering our best performance. And now I just don't think I can do that any more.

"It's over for professional sport, but I don't think you ever truly stop."

Brownlee said the birth of his son Freddie 10 months ago clarified his plans for the future.

"I don't think I can have that commitment because of how life is. He's my priority now, my family, but also with my body as well," said Brownlee.

"The thought of missing a training session used to be the worst thing in the world, whereas now, if Freddie is ill or needs me, then without question I do that.

"I used to have absolutely no fear with racing. I used to dive into corners on my bike at 60kph and not care.

"If I hit that corner and crash, then I can't hold Freddie for five to six weeks if I have got a broken wrist. I was asking if that was really worth it any more."

articles.title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme El Niño weather, minister says
articles.text:
Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".

Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.

The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.

Dame Angela said, external: "We're about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

"It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

"If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't.

"So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."

Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.

The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply.

It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.

It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.

articles.title: Xbox to limit cloud gaming to 15 hours a month for Game Pass users
articles.text:
Xbox is introducing strict monthly time limits for Game Pass subscribers who stream games online through its cloud gaming service.

The changes, which come into effect in November, will see a subscriber to the £16.99 Ultimate monthly plan able to stream games for up to 15 hours a month - before having to purchase additional cloud play time.

Xbox said the limits were due to the rising cost of cloud gaming, and they would allow the firm to "continue to invest" in the service's "reliability and performance".

While some questioned, external whether the service was used by many to begin with, others called out, external the additional limits for subscribers.

Cloud gaming allows players to stream and play games online from a remote server using a phone, tablet or controller, rather than downloading and running it on a PC or console at home.

Different tiers of subscription to Game Pass will have different limits.

Premium users will get 10 hours, while those on the basic Essential tier will get five hours a month before they have to pay for extra time.

Xbox claimed just 4% of the people who use Games Pass - its Netflix-style subscription plan for games - use its cloud gaming service.

A recent Wall Street Journal article, external reported Game Pass has 30 million subscribers, which would leave the number of people affected by the cloud gaming changes at roughly 1.2 million.

"This is a pretty awful change, hopefully Xbox adds an extra zero on the end cause 15hrs is abysmal. 30 minutes a day, really?" posted one commenter on X, external.

Jez Corden of Windows Central told the BBC the announcement showed that "absolutely nothing is safe from the AI-driven component crisis," but he added it also highlighted "where Microsoft's priorities are".

Both cloud gaming and AI use data centres to process information.

"For them to continue to offer unlimited access to Microsoft Copilot [AI] for free but restrict paid cloud gaming in this way shows some contradiction," he added.

Xbox said in a blog post, external that from November, users would also be able to use the company's cloud gaming feature without subscribing to Game Pass, but by buying "cloud playtime hours" through the Xbox store.

It has not revealed how much extra hours of cloud gaming would cost.

The news comes as Asha Sharma, Xbox's chief executive, told the BBC in an exclusive recent interview that the company and the industry as a whole needed to "start to innovate on affordability and efficiency," amid a "crisis" in computing prices.

"As an industry, we're in the middle of 'Rampocalypse'. We're in the middle of people coming back from Covid and the patterns changing," she said.

"Rampocalypse" refers to the fact that the cost of a previously cheap hardware component, random access memory (Ram), has shot up in price with the expansion of compute-hungry data centres. Some people also call it "Ramageddon".

Sharma added: "Within Xbox, we haven't been healthy. And so a lot of the reset that will take us throughout the year is really meant to help ensure that we are here for the next 25 years and we're continuing to serve our purpose and our mission."

According to Xbox owner Microsoft's July financial filings, external, annual Xbox revenue dropped by $1.7bn to roughly $21.8bn (£16.1bn) - a 7% decline from 2025.

Part of Sharma's reset has seen 3,200 people let go at the company - with 1,600 job losses announced in July, and the remaining posts to go gradually over the course of Microsoft's 2027 financial year.

Studios which had been acquired by Xbox - including Compulsion Games, which made the Bafta-winning South of Midnight and Double Fine Productions, makers of Psychonauts - were also made independent again.

Sharma is betting these changes can reverse its fortunes despite concerns over its subscription strategy and rising AI-related costs.

"Sometimes you have to restructure a business when it's not doing well, and that was true with our Xbox business," Microsoft's president Brad Smith recently told the BBC.

articles.title: Jobseekers warned over online interview and recruitment scams
articles.text:
Jobseekers are being warned to be vigilant as scammers are targeting people on job listings websites to trick them into downloading bogus interview tools.

One victim was invited on LinkedIn by a fake recruiter to take part in a job interview process and downloaded a normal-looking document which turned out to be malicious software.

Within hours the hackers had drained his cryptocurrency accounts of £18,000 of savings and disappeared.

"It's a horrible feeling to be out a substantial amount - something I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy," the victim, who wanted to stay anonymous, said.

Professional recruitment platforms LinkedIn and Indeed have warned of growing numbers of job scams in recent months.

LinkedIn released data highlighting what it called The Gen Z "Scam Gap", external - "Younger professionals face the highest exposure to scams (32%), yet nearly a third (32%) admit to ignoring red flags due to a competitive job market."

When approached by the BBC, the company said in a crowded and competitive job market, "many young people feel they can't afford to be skeptical... because they feel opportunities are so scarce".

The platform pointed to advice on its website, external about how to spot recruitment scams by, for example, verifying that the company and job was real and doing thorough research before engaging in talks.

The victim - who lost their savings after being hacked - had handed in their notice and made it clear on LinkedIn that they were looking for a new job.

A fake recruiter sent them a potential job offer and held a video call about the job before asking them to carry out a standard technical assessment, with instructions on the Google Sheet document.

But the document was laced with malicious software.

After completing the task, the candidate went to bed and woke up to find their online wallets emptied of their savings.

"I wiped my computer and changed all my passwords and was exhausted emotionally and mentally drained," they said.

"I felt a mixture of disbelief and anger - at the hackers and at myself. I was also confused until I figured out how they had got me."

Cyber-security researchers from Have I Been Squatted carried out an analysis of how the attack worked and say the new wave of recruitment scams are hard to spot.

"This wasn't a badly written email with a suspicious attachment - this person was walked through what looked like a real job interview, on real Google pages, behind a real Google login, and the software they were asked to install was digitally signed like any legitimate app," said chief executive Juxhin D Brigjaj.

The case comes as others have reported similar attacks through the job listing platform Indeed, which put out advice in July about avoiding scams, external.

Criminals are using the pressure and excitement of job interviews to lure people into downloading booby-trapped mobile applications like a fake Indeed Interview app or one called MyInterview.

According to cyber-security company Malwarebytes, the fake recruiters use lures such as: "Complete your interview by installing the Indeed app" or "salary agreement available after app installation".

Once downloaded the malicious apps allow hackers to access private data for extortion or to use in financial attacks.

"Interviewing through Indeed's platform happens entirely in a browser and never requires downloading a special app," Indeed recently posted online.

"Any message asking a job seeker to download an app to participate in an interview is not legitimate."
